b. Board of Supervisor's Roles & Responsibilities:
Bryan Layton talked about the organizational chart that was created and
will be put on the website.  He acknowledged everyone who has helped
through the transition of him taking over as County Manager.
A presentation was shown.  Rochelle Lacapa talked about roles and
responsibilities going into an election year and campaign season,
including public officials vs. private citizens.  She indicated that those
running, that hold a public office, need to be more mindful of what they are
doing while campaigning.  She stated that public resources can’t be used
for campaigning, including facilities, equipment, personnel, or supplies.
She talked about how defining when they are on campaign time versus
county time, helps maintain the trust of the public and transparency.  She
stated that when going through the statute, campaign finance law, and the
policies and procedures, there’s a gap in information around the topic.
She has reached out to CSA and other counties to see if there was
1 of 8 
DRAFT

<!-- page 8 -->
anything that clearly defines ethics or the law when campaigning if you’re
an elected officer.  She indicated that our policies manual covers political
activities for employees but that there is a disclaimer that elected officials
are excluded.  She talked about potentially changing that if they wanted it
to include the Elected Officials.  She indicated that a helpful tool for staff
would be to clarify on their calendar when they are taking personal time
for campaigning.  She indicated that the House Ethics Committee uses a
guidebook for what elected officials can and can’t do and talked about how
they decipher their time on their calendars. 
She talked about how some efficiencies can be built into the policies and
procedures to help with the gap of information, including the Chair’s
agenda for how meetings are run and the Board policies, that were
adopted in 2009 which outline what the Boards roles are.  She further
talked about whether there is a need to revise the Board’s policies, a new
Code of Ethics, revise the personal policies manual or if there are other
options the Board would like to establish.  She indicated that this could
establish a guide for future supervisors coming in, to help them with how
the county operates and what their role is within the county.  She
requested feedback on if there is a need for these things to be updated
and who should work on the updates. 
Supervisor Whiting stated that he likes the idea of staff working on
recommendations.  He indicated that it would create an expectation for the
Board around actions and communication when engaging with the public
and each other.  He further indicated that it would be a good way of
onboarding newly elected officials and/or a yearly refresher. 
Supervisor Seymore stated that this is something we should have in
place, that it doesn’t need to be recreated, but that we should explore
what works well in other counties when restructuring it. 
A discussion was held regarding what would be included in the board
policies, including the vetting process for requests from the public for
placement of items on the agenda; items being on the consent agenda
versus the regular agenda; formalities for the meeting including time
allotted for call to the public or public comments on an item, where in the
agenda comments should be made and if time should be yielded and not
allowing jump drives from outside of the county to be used on county
computers.     
Ms. Lacapa thanked them for the conversation, indicating that it is helpful
for staff to know what to incorporate into the board policies when updating
and provides clarity for staff and the public. 
Supervisor Seymore talked about the Board currently being elected on
the same cycle and possibly looking at staggard terms in the future. 
Supervisor Benally requested a copy of guidelines for campaigning for
elected officials. 
A discussion was held regarding being ethical while campaigning as an
Elected Official.

c. Public Works Update:
A presentation was shown. Madhav Mundle highlighted some of the major
accomplishments from the past year, including purchase of equipment,
paving and gravel projects, adoption of the new building permit fee
schedule and being able to reduce building permit approval times.  He
stated that staff is working with a vendor to create a portal so that
applications can be submitted online.
Mr. Mundle answered questions regarding the reduced time for permitting. 
Supervisor Seymore addressed the time reduction and indicated that the
department has done a great job. 
Mr. Mundle continued to address major accomplishments, including,
getting approval for a hearing officer for code compliance and approval of
a new ordinance for wireless cell towers.  He talked about the
accomplishment of receiving funding through HURF Exchange, AZ
SMART, the Highway Safety Improvement Program, Off System Bridge
and CDBG funding. 
Supervisor Benally inquired which of the funds could be utilized on tribal
land.
Mr. Mundle stated that AZ SMART and Off System Bridge are not
available on tribal lands unless they apply for it on their own and that
HURF Exchange is exclusively for Navajo County facilities. 
Supervisor Benally inquired what the end of county-maintenance means,
indicating that it’s her understanding that the county doesn’t own any
roads.
A discussion was held regarding county roads versus roads on tribal land,
the funding for roadways and what roads can be maintained. 
Supervisor Whitesinger talked about the partnerships that are needed
for requests to help with road maintenance. 
Supervisor Benally talked about how she has requested assistance on
tribal roads and has not received the assistance she requested. 
Supervisor Whiting indicated that this sounds like a district specific issue
that needs to be worked through with Public Works.  He talked about the
need to have a meeting with tribal leaders regarding partnerships. 
Mr. Mundle continued to address the accomplishments in Public Works,
such as the 5-year capital improvement projects and the pavement
management program.  He talked about road health checks, indicating
that the pavement management program is only for paved roads, that it is
needed, that it’s a pilot program to see if it will work and he inquired if the
program should continue if it is cost effective and makes economic sense
and which roads that it should be used on.  He addressed the cost for
maintaining the roads. 
Supervisor Whitesinger inquired about cost effectiveness. 
Mr. Mundle indicated that they are working on that, that the first program
had a lot of inefficiencies, that the more work done the better it will be and
that they plan to do it on low volume and low speed roads. 
A discussion was held on the roads and the costs for maintenance. 
Supervisor Seymore stated that it’s great to know the conditions of the
roads and indicated that it’s an asset to the county. 
Mr. Mundle talked about challenges and how to proceed. 
Mr. Layton talked about how the experience and connections Mr. Mundle
has with ADOT has brought in new things for Navajo County and thanked

e. Financial Sustainability and Outlook:
Jayson Vowell stated the county is in a good solid financial position
considering where it was at 5 years ago.  He reviewed the FY23 budgeted
revenues vs. actual revenues and budgeted expenditures vs. actual
expenditures.  He talked about the normal cost of doing business,
including market fluctuations, professional service increases, changes to
revenue streams/cost share, capital outlay and labor.  He talked about the
differences that have affected the budget from 2019 to current for the
expenditures and revenues, indicating that going forward they would like
to see it start to flatten out and be more consistent.  He talked about
property taxes and keeping the rate flat.  He spoke about where the
revenues come from, including sales tax, county sales tax and property
tax plus some federal state money from intergovernmental agreements. 
He talked about the future focus for organizational maintenance, including
a pay plan, COLA and performance pay; new hires; increase to capital
outlay, including investments in technology, building repairs and
modernization, building replacement/expansion and vehicles and
equipment; and subscriptions vs. a one-time purchase.
Supervisor Seymore talked about being able to retain the employees that
we have by keeping up with performance pay and salaries.  He addressed
the need to do upgrades due to the buildings being outdated and for
  
                                                                    5 of 8 
DRAFT

<!-- page 12 -->
having subscriptions versus one-time purchases for equipment.  He
addressed budgeting versus using the reserves for different needs. 
Supervisor Whitesinger talked about investments that have been made
over the past years and the position that we are sitting in now compared
to in the past, indicating that we need to be prepared for the continued
cost increase for everything. 
Mr. Vowell talked about the steps taken to make salaries competitive,
indicating that they don’t want to have to do another market upgrade after
the work put in with the adjustments they have made.  He indicated, from
a budget perspective, each department needs to know that they will be
paying more in the future for the different tools that they use. 
Supervisor Whitesinger indicated that they don’t want to be put in a
position of having to look at layoffs of cutting back, but that they want to be
able to continue to provide the services that are needed.
Mr. Layton talked about the work that has been done to make the pay
competitive, investing in the employees, and about the cultural
environment being made to help employees want to stay.  He addressed
the things that they want to do to help employees show that they are
valued and recognized.
Mr. Vowell indicated that they will be looking at FY25 soon and indicated
that when going into the next budget cycle they want to get feedback on
the process and determine if they should keep as is or make changes.
A discussion was held about some possible changes that could be made
such as getting more input from the departments on what they are asking. 
Mr. Vowell thanked the Board, indicating that he appreciates their
guidance and the tone that they set for the organization.     
 
f. Public Health Service Delivery & County Facility Planning: 
Mr. Layton stated that when looking at renovations and facility upgrades,
they were looking to increase, promote and improve access to the county
as well as make it safe and secure for both employees and customers in
an affordable way.  He reviewed the current county projects, such as
customer access, the restrooms, a breakroom, and a training room, the
repair to the sewer pipes, the modernization of the superior courtrooms for
technology and furniture, the upgrade to the county internet, the
organization of records retention, the upgrade to the fire alarm, offering
CPR/First Aid classes to all employees, emergency signage, adding
shade sails to the outdoor areas for breaks, repurposing the basketball
court and put up shade pavilions, outdoor picnic seating and paint the
markings for pickleball courts.  He talked about some proposed projects
that they are looking at such as solar protection for vehicles/equipment, he
talked about the benefits for the solar covered parking; the proposal for the
branding/color options for the seal and the proposed monument
signage. 
A discussion was held regarding the proposed monuments and the
different options. 
Mr. Layton talked about turning the area into a place where people can
stop and take pictures.  He talked about the next steps for the proposed
projects.  He addressed long term needs for the county, including
necessary expansions at the Sheriff’s Office and Public Health; the
necessity for creating another courtroom; the need for professional office

Supervisor Benally inquired if there is space to be able to expand at the

1. Presentation of the WIC Baby Shower special event that was held on
September 29, 2023: 
Kelsey Nies talked about her position in the WIC office.  She talked about
the community baby shower that was held, indicating that they received a
special project grant from the Arizona WIC office to be able to hold the
event, which was the first of its kind in our county.  She reviewed the
WIC values, including the benefits of breastfeeding and the importance of
education and support.  She talked about the project goals of the event,
which included to support, inform, and empower pregnant and new
mothers, their support person, and their breastfeeding journey; establish
peer connections; and gain new WIC clients.  She talked about the
community baby shower that was held on September 29 in Show Low,
indicating that they were awarded $3,125 to put the event on, had some
informational WIC booths and community partner booths and provided
breastfeeding goodie bags to all who attended and had raffle prizes.  She
stated that they served thirty-one families, that they had nine new clients
that registered, that they had approximately eighty total attendees, and
they were able to make referrals for car seat/ pack n’ play training and
dental.  She talked about strengths from the event, including peer
connections, referrals, attendance, and then lessons learned were that
rushes were difficult to manage and the weather.  She indicated that
moving forward they will collaborate with tribal and community partners
and expand the event to other locations in Navajo County.
Supervisor Seymore thanked Ms. Nies for the report and for her
excitement and enthusiasm.
Vice-Chairman Whiting thanked Ms. Nies and those that were involved
for looking at out of the box ways to serve communities in ways that
matter.

Consideration of adoption of Resolution Number 34-2023, adopting the
new voting precincts maps and polling places that were adjusted to meet
the new Board of Supervisor Districts pursuant to A.R.S. §16-411 : 
A presentation was shown. Jason Moore talked about the requirements
for drawing precinct lines pursuant to ARS 16-411(A)(1).  He addressed
the areas of agreement, stating that the precinct lines that are drawn
can’t include more than one Congressional district, one Legislative
district, one Board of Supervisors district and one Justice of the Peace
  
                                                                    4 of 13 
DRAFT

<!-- page 19 -->
district, one Board of Supervisors district and one Justice of the Peace
district and that the special taxing districts are not considered when
drawing the lines.  He talked about the areas of disagreements, including
if a precinct can include a municipality and unincorporated area, if it can
include more than one municipality and if it can include more than one
school district.   He addressed the requirements for boundaries pursuant
to the law, regarding precincts being drawn within election districts of
election officers for the state, political subdivisions, and community
college districts. He addressed those who have election districts.  He
indicated that school districts and cities and towns are political
subdivisions that are not divided into election districts, that there is an
exception by statute that allows a school district to divide the district itself
into a single member district, but that those don’t exist in Navajo County. 
He talked about how Maricopa County does their precincts.  He
addressed issues when applying ARS 16-311(K)(1), which is found in
Chapter 3, Article 2 of Title 16, indicating that it governs the nomination,
filing out nomination papers and circulation of the candidate nomination
petitions.  He talked about school districts and the city and town
elections.  He stated after the last Board meeting, he looked at all of the
northern tier counties in Arizona and he provided information on how
Gila, Coconino, and Yavapai Counties create their boundaries.  He
stated that there is no limit on the number of people that can be included
in a precinct under the statute, but that it is at the discretion of the Board
regarding the number of precincts there are. 
   
Chairman Peshlakai opened the meeting for public comments.

precincts are drawn.  She talked about the areas that should have
additional polling places due to the number of voters. She recommended
that what is being presented today not be approved due to insufficient
information. 
The public hearing was closed.

previous one being outdated and addressed concerns with some of the
speed changes in that area.  He indicated that it’s a project that’s
designed, that it has been a length of time to get going, but that the area
will be developed eventually.  He indicated that there needs to be a time
frame for phase one and to make sure that there are assurances for
completion of the project for sewer and water.
Vice-Chairman Whiting addressed the improvements in the plan and
indicated that he likes the direction that it’s moving in.  He talked about
the increase for the population in the area, indicating that he agrees that
a traffic study needs to be done.  He inquired if there were any public
meetings held.
Mr. Loper stated that there were no public meetings, that outreach went
with Navajo County requirements and until the Planning & Zoning
Commission meeting, they did have any response from the posting and
mailing notice that went out.  He indicated that comments that were made
                                                                    11 of 13 
DRAFT

<!-- page 26 -->
by Ms. Westover at the Commission hearing.
Supervisor Whiting addressed having a public hearing and inquired if
the applicant would be willing to do that.
Mr. Loper indicated that they can if that is what the Board would like, and
that they could try and have it prior to the next board meeting, but that
they don’t want to push it out too far due to the holidays. 
Supervisor Whiting inquired if staff would be willing to help with the
process for a public meeting.
Ms. Starke stated that some of the concerns listed have been resolved
as conditions in the staff report.  She indicated that staff would support
the wish of the Board for the public hearing. 
Vice-Chairman Whiting made a motion to table the item until after the
applicant has had an opportunity to do a public hearing, motion
seconded by Supervisor Seymore.  Vote unanimous approving the
motion. 
 
7. COUNTY BUSINESS UPDATE: Report from County Manager, County
Attorney and Board members :
Brad Carlyon reminded the Board that registration for NACo is open. 
Bryan Layton reminded all employees of the Navajo County Health Fair
that is happening today.
Supervisor Benally reported on the Rural Transportation Summit that
she attended, indicating that she got information on grants that will be
available to tribal areas.  She stated that at the Chapter levels she has
been working on a resolution for the Black Mesa and Kayenta areas for a
rural transportation bus route study and that she will be meeting with
NACOG next week.  She stated that she will be meeting with NDOT and
BIA to discuss road priorities for the Pinon and Black Mesa Chapter
areas.  She addressed the area that is supposed to be being paved but
indicated that it is being held up due to archeological issues.  She stated
that she has been attending Chapter Meetings in her District and the
Winslow City Council Meeting. 
Chairman Peshlakai reported on attending meetings in his District, both
Chapter and Tribal.  He indicated that he appreciates staffs help with the
partnerships.  He talked about the pamphlet that staff created, indicating
that it has been helpful and that those that he has given them to have
really appreciated the information.  He thanked the Recorder’s Office for
the information provided on elections and pamphlets on voter
registration. He stated that yesterday he was a Guest Speaker for Red
Ribbon Week at Indian Wells Elementary. 
 
ADJOURN:  11:44 a.m. meeting adjourned.

Board of Supervisors Regular 2. f.        
Meeting Date: 11/14/2023  
Title: Governor's Office of Highway Safety DUI Contract 2024-405d-025
Submitted For: David Clouse, Sheriff 
Submitted By: Kimberley Willis, Sheriff's Office Finance Manager
Department: Sheriff 
Motion before the Board:
Award from Governor's Office of Highway Safety Contract 2024-405d-025 for DUI/Impaired
Driving Enforcement
Background:
The Navajo County Sheriff's Office has been awarded $33,600 for DUI enforcement overtime
efforts and related materials. This award includes $24,000.00 in overtime salary and ERE and
$9,600.00 for the purchase of 2 Sotoxa Mobile Test Systems along with the annual maintenance
fees. Sotoxa Test Systems are distributed by Intoximeter and test for six different drug classes.
GOHS reimburses overtime costs at 100% and ERE up to 40%. The grant period runs from
October 1, 2023 to September 30, 2024.

Board of Supervisors Regular 2. i.        
Meeting Date: 11/14/2023  
Title: FY24 Arizona Attorney General's Victims' Rights Program Grant Award
Submitted For: Brad Carlyon, County Attorney  Submitted By: Lynda Young, Office
Manager
Department: County Attorney
Motion before the Board:
Acceptance and approval of the FY24 Arizona Attorney General's Office's Victims' Rights
program grant agreement
Background:
Funds from this grant, provided over 12,000 mandated notifications to victims in fiscal year
2023. Notifications to victims ranged from legal updates to case status to notifications of rights
due to the victim as a result of victimization. Specifically, funds pay the partial salary of two
Office Support Specialists that are part of the Notification process. There is no match
requirement with this grant.
Fiscal Impact
Fiscal Year: FY24
Budgeted Y/N: Y
Amount Requested: $26,800.00
Fiscal Impact:
$18,760.00 towards salary and $8,040.00 towards ERE.  No match requirement.

Board of Supervisors Regular 2. m.        
Meeting Date: 11/14/2023  
Title: Contract Amendment to Contract with eX2 for the Design, Construction,
Maintenance and Marketing of Fiber Optic Infrastructure
Submitted For: Grant Evans, Capital Projects Manager 
Submitted By: Grant Evans, Capital Projects Manager
Department: Public Works
Motion before the Board:
Amendment No. 1 to Contract with eX2 for the Design, Construction, Maintenance and
Marketing of Fiber Optic Infrastructure to revise the scope of work and increase the contract
amount for value-added design changes and for additional environmental permitting
requirements
Background:
On February 28, 2023, the Board approved a Contract with eX2 Technology, LLC (eX2) for the
Design, Construction, Maintenance and Marketing of Fiber Optic Infrastructure.  This contract
amendment is in the form of two change orders - change orders number 1 and 2.
Change Order #1 provides for design changes that were made to increase the conduit and fiber
sizes for the laterals off of the middle mile backbone that will serve our County-owned
facilities. Change order #1 also provides for an increased handhole size for (43) of the
handholes in the project.  These larger handholes are being placed at the splice locations
throughout the project.  Both of these changes, constituting change order #1, further enhance
the project for future expansion and capacity. 
Change Order #2 is necessary to meet all the environmental clearance requirements of the
permitting agencies, including the Arizona Department of Transportation (ADOT), Bureau of
Land Management (BLM), United States Forest Service (USFS) and Arizona State Land
Department (ASLD). The environmental clearance requirements required by each agency are
more than initially anticipated by eX2. There are significant additional cultural resource field
surveys needed, additional native plant surveys, and environmental support to assist the USFS
to keep the permitting schedule from being delayed on USFS lands. While the total amount of
the change order for the increased environmental work totals $307, 017.46, plus an additional
allowance of $92, 166.81, this equates to slightly less than $3,000/mile for the 105 mile project.
eX2's original contract pricing of $47,240 for environmental assumed minimal environmental
work and a Class I evaluation. Due to the age of previous environmental surveys and known
cultural and biological concerns, a Class III survey, requiring significant field work, is
required.  Also included in change order #2 is an allowance of $92,166.81 that will only be
used, as needed, for monitoring of cultural sites during construction.

<!-- page 541 -->
Staff has negotiated both change order number 1 and change order number 2 and agrees they are
fair and reasonable for the services provided.
 
Fiscal Impact
Fiscal Year: FY24 & 25
Budgeted Y/N: Y
Amount Requested: 471,087.99
Fiscal Impact:
Funds will come from the Local Assistance Consistency Fund.

AZTEC Scope of Services  2  November 1, 2023 
Navajo County Broadband – Environmental Support 
AZTEC Project Number: AZENS2320‐04 
 
SCOPE OF SERVICES & COST ESTIMATE 
eX2 Technology LLC 
Navajo County Broadband – Environmental Support 
AZTEC Project Number: AZENS2320‐04 
1.   Task Understanding 
eX2  Technology  LLC  (Client)  has  requested  this  modification  of  scope  of  services  and  cost  to  assist  in  fulfilling 
various  agency  environmental  requirements  for  a  fiber  optic  project  being  administered  by  Navajo  County  in 
A r i z o n a .  T h e  p r o j e c t  w o u l d  i n v o l v e  t h e  i n s t a l l a t i o n  o f  a p p r o x i mately  107  miles  of  new  fiber  optic  lines  and 
associated  boxes  within  Arizona Department  of  Transportation  (ADOT)  right‐of‐way  (ROW)  and/or  easement 
through  Bureau  of  Land  Management  (BLM),  Arizona  State  Land  Department  (ASLD),  and  Apache‐Sitgreaves 
N a t i o n a l  F o r e s t  ( A S N F ) ,  a s  w e l l  a s  a  s e c t i o n  o f  f i b e r  o u t s i d e  of  ADOT’s  ROW/easement  along  Navajo  County 
maintained roads through ASNF. The project would be broken up into six segments with fiber optic lines primarily 
installed along Interstate 40,  State Route (SR) 77, and SR 260.  The segment locations within ADOTs ROW are as 
follows: 
 Segment 1 (APS Connection) – Along State Route (SR) 40 from approximate milepost (MP) 278 to 
the intersection of SR 77 
 Segment 2 (Holbrook to Snowflake) – Along SR 77 from approximate MP 360 to MP 388 
 Segment 3 (Snowflake to Show Low, and Lone Pine Road) – Along S R 77 from approximate MP 
349 to MP 360, and along SR 260 from approximate MP 335 to MP 338 
 Segment 4 (Show Low to Pinetop) – Along SR 260 from approximate MP 342 to 353 
 Segment 5 (Pinetop to Reservation Border) – Along SR 260 from approximate MP 353 to MP 356 
 Segment 6 (Show Low to Heber Overgaard) Along SR 260 from approximate MP 306 to MP 335 
 
The initial scope of services AZTEC provided the Client was foc used on assistance with environmental needs in 
association with obtaining ADOT encroachment permits for the portions of the project which cross ADOT right‐of‐
way or easement. Subsequent coor dination with the various invol ved agencies (ASLD, ASNF, and BLM) identified 
the need for several additional environmental tasks to satisfy permitting requirements.

 Surveys will be conducted in accordance with the ASLD Native Plant Survey Protocol that is outlined in the

(MA2) (Hendricks 1985).  
 No more than four (4) sample points will be required.  
 The  surveys  would  remain  within  ADOT’s  highway  easements.  AZTEC w o u l d  b e  a b l e  t o  u s e  o u r  A D O T

Native Plant Survey Scope of Work 
 Complete a Native Plant Survey at four (4) sample points on ASLD lands within the project area.

change through the process described in Arizona Board of Regents rules implementing A.R.S. § 15-1631 (as 
amended) and can be adjusted based on increased efficiencies or developing needs. 
 
f. Timelines for quotes, invoices, receiving payment, scheduling services: 
• All quote requests submitted to the ASM Request Quote for Services website are reviewed by ASM 
personnel for compliance with Arizona Antiquities Act. The quote is emailed to the requestor within two 
business days, unless feedback is necessary. If a Value-added service is requested, the customized quote 
may require more than two business days to complete. Once the quote is approved, an invoice is issued 
within two business days of quote approval. 
 
• Credit Card Payments that are received before 4pm MST (Arizona Time) on regular business days will be 
posted the day they are received. Credit Card Payments received after 4pm MST (Arizona Time), will be 
posted on the next regular business day. Check payments are posted the same business day received in the 
RII Business Center. 
 
• ASM services are scheduled once payment and all appropriate forms are received. If an expedited service 
has not been selected, services are usually delivered within 20 business days.

 CONTRACT FOR PROFESSIONAL SERVICES  
 
 
AGREEMENT made as of November 3, 2023, between Navajo County ("County") 
and Ironside Engineering & Development (“Consultant”). 
 
WHEREAS, County requires certain professional services for Skylane Road Topo 
Survey Project (“Project”); and 
 
WHEREAS, Consultant represents that it has the necessary expertise to provide such 
services in accordance with the terms of this Agreement. 
 
NOW, THEREFORE, the parties agree as follows: 
 
1. Services.  Consultant shall perform the work described in the Scope of Work dated 
October 18, 2023, and those additional items set forth in the Consultant’s schedule 
and fee proposal dated October 18, 2023, in a competent and professional manner to 
the satisfaction of County.  The Scope of Work and the Consultant’s schedule and fee 
proposal are attached hereto and by this reference incorporat ed herein.  If any 
incorporated term is inconsistent with the Agreement, this Agreement shall control.   
 
2. Consultant’s Expertise.  Consultant warrants that it has the ability, authority, 
capacity and professional expertise to perfo rm this Agreement.  Consultant shall 
provide an adequate staff of experienced  personnel, capable of and devoted to the 
successful accomplishment of the work to be performed hereunder.  Consultant shall 
assign specific individuals to key positio ns.  Once assigned to work under this 
Agreement, key personnel shall not be removed or replaced without County’s prior 
written approval.  
 
3. Independent Contractor.  Consultant acknowledges that  it is an independent 
contractor.  Neither party is or shall purport to be an agent, employee, partner, joint 
venturer or associate of the other.  An employee or agen t of one party shall not be 
deemed an employer or agent  of the other party for any purpose.  Taxes or Social 
Security contributions will not be with held from any payment by County, and 
Consultant shall be solely responsible for such matters.

4. Subcontracts.  Consultant shall not enter into any subcontract with respect to any of 
the work to be performed hereunder without County’s prior written approval.  All 
subcontracts shall comply with applicable federal and state laws and regulations and 
shall impose on the subcontractor substantially the same obligations as are imposed 
on Consultant by this Agreement with respect to those matters covered by Sections 8, 
9, 10, 12, 15 and 18.  Consultant is  responsible for full performance of this 
Agreement regardless of whether subcontractors are used. 
 
5. Time for Completion.  Consultant’s services will be provided in a manner consistent 
with the degree of care and skill ordi narily exercised by me mbers of the same 
profession currently practicing under similar circumstances.  Consultant’s services 
shall be performed as expeditiously as is consistent with professional skill and care 
and the orderly progress of the Project, and in accord ance with an agreed upon 
schedule for the performance of the Services hereunder.  Time limits established by a 
schedule approved by County shall not, except for reasonable cause, be exceeded by 
County or Consultant.  The Schedule shall be adjusted, if  necessary, as the Project 
proceeds.  The date for final performance shall be extended by the number of days 
that performance is delayed by governmental approval or review procedures or other 
causes beyond Consultant’s reasonable control, as jointly confirmed in writing by the 
parties’ representatives. 
 
6. Payment.  County shall pay to Consultant a not-to-exceed sum of three thousand 
eight hundred dollars ($3,800.0 0) as payment in full fo r all services rendered by 
Consultant pursuant to this Agreement.  Pa yments shall be made within 30 days of 
County’s receipt of Consultant’s monthly invoices.  Each invoice shall detail the work 
performed during the billing period.  Invoice amounts in percent of Project cost shall 
not exceed the percentage of completion of the Project as approved by County.   
 
7. Defects in Work.  County may reject any work product that fails to meet customary 
professional standards or Project specifi cations.  Consultant agrees to promptly 
remedy all such deficiencies.  The parties shall make a good faith effort to resolve any 
controversy or claim through informal nego tiation as set forth in Section 12.  No 
compensation shall be paid for any reject ed work until such issues have been 
resolved. 
 
8. Insurance Requirements.   
 
A. Consultant shall maintain in effect , at all times during the term of this 
Agreement, insurance adequate to protect County and its agents, 
representatives, officers, officials and employees against such losses as set 
forth below.  Consultant shall provide County with a current Certificate of 
Insurance or a certified copy of the insurance policy naming County as an 
additional insured (except for Errors an d Omissions / Professional Liability 
coverage). 
 
 
B. The following types an d amounts of insurance are required as minimums:

9. Indemnity.  To the fullest extent allowable  by law, Consultant shall defend, 
indemnify and hold harmless County and its  representatives, officers, officials and 
employees (the “Indemnitees”) from and against any and all claims, damages, losses 
and expenses (including but not limited to attorney fees, court costs, and the costs of

negligent acts, errors, mistakes or omissions in the performance of this Agreement.

by any person for whose negligent acts, errors, mistakes or omissions Consultant may 
be liable) to the extent of Consultant’s negligence or fault.  The amount and type of 
insurance coverage requirements set fort h above shall not lim it the scope of the

11. Non-Assignment.  Consultant shall not assign any right or interest in this Agreement 
without County’s prior written approval, nor  shall Consultant delegate any duty 
hereunder without County’s prior written approval.   
 
12. Negotiation of Disputes.  The parties shall make a good faith effort to resolve any 
claim or controversy or claim through informal negotiation.  Notice of any claim or 
controversy shall be provided in writi ng, with supporting doc umentation, to the 
recipient designated in Section 21.  The recipient shall have seven calendar days to 
prepare and deliver a written response.  If the parties fail to resolve the disputes 
within a reasonable period of not less than ten days, either party may pursue available 
legal remedies. 
 
13. Suspension and Termination by County: 
 
A. Suspension.  County may, without cause, order Consultant in writing to suspend, 
delay or interrupt its performance in whole or part.  An adjustment shall be made 
to the completion date and for any increase in the cost of performance resulting 
from the suspension, delay or interruption.  No adjustment shall be made to the 
extent that performance is or would have been suspended, delayed or interrupted 
by another cause for which Consultant is responsible. 
 
B. Termination for Cause.   County may terminate th is Agreement for cause if 
Consultant refuses or fails to supply enough properly skilled workers to perform 
this Agreement; fails to make required payments to subcontractors; disregards 
laws, ordinances, rules, regulations or  orders of a public  authority having 
jurisdiction; or otherwise commits a material breach of  this Agreement.  When 
any of the foregoing causes exist, County shall give Consultant written notice and 
a ten-day opportunity to cure the default.  If the default remains uncured, County 
may (without prejudice to any other rights or remedies it may have) terminate this 
Agreement and finish the work or cause it to be finished.  If the unpaid balance of 
the Agreement exceeds the cost of fini shing the work (including any expenses 
incurred by County as a result of Cons ultant’s default), C onsultant shall be 
entitled to payment for its performance up to the amount of such excess.  If the 
cost of finishing the work exceeds the u npaid balance, Consultant shall pay the 
difference to County. 
 
C. Termination for Convenience.   County, by written n otice to Consultant, may 
terminate this Agreement in whole or part when in the sole discretion of County it 
is in County’s best interests to do so.  Consultant shall be pa id for all material, 
equipment and services provided, as well as reasonable termination expenses and 
a reasonable allowance for profit and overhead, provided that such payments, 
exclusive of termination expenses, shal l not exceed the total amount payable 
pursuant to Section 6 less any paymen ts previously made to Consultant.

services which were not provided. 
 
D. Consultant’s Responsibilities.  Upon receipt of a termination notice, Consultant

Dear Mr. Madril,   
 
Navajo County would like to request approval for two Pickle Ball Courts to be installed at the Tall 
Timbers Park in Overgaard. Although the exact location of the courts has not been identified, the 
court will be within the boundaries of the existing park.  
 
Navajo County intends to partner with the Heber-Overgaard Chamber to include this improvement 
to the Tall Timbers Park. Many community members have expressed an interest in pickle ball 
courts and will be an added value to the community. This improvement will greatly enhance the 
Heber-Overgaard extra-curricular activities within the community.  
 
Navajo County currently has a Special Use Permit for the construction, operation and maintenance 
of this park which will expire December 31, 2025. We currently have a  request in to extend that 
permit.  
 
Please give full consideration to this request, as this assistance will be of great benefit to our 
communities.

Title: National Native American Heritage Month 2023
Submitted By: Melissa Buckley, Clerk of the Board of Supervisors
Department: Board of Supervisors
Presented By: Supervisor Dawnafe
Whitesinger/Miss WMA Queen
1st Attendant Charity Johnson
Motion before the Board:
Consideration of a Proclamation declaring November 2023 as "National Native American
Heritage Month"
Background:
On August 3, 1990, President of the United States George H.W. Bush declared the month of
November as National American Indian Heritage Month, thereafter commonly referred to as
National Native American Heritage Month.
Recommendation: 
Staff recommends approval
Attachments
Native American Heritage Proclamation 
Form Review
Form Started By: Donna Hurstrom Started On: 11/26/2018 07:35 AM
Final Approval Date: 10/30/2023

<!-- page 586 -->
Navajo County 
Proclamation 
 
NOVEMBER 2023 
“NATIONAL NATIVE AMERICAN HERITAGE MONTH” 
 
WHEREAS, During National Native American Heritage Month , we recognize the 
invaluable contributions of all Native communities that have shaped our country; and  
 
WHEREAS, National Native American Heritage Month  is celebrated every year to 
recognize Native American cultures, contributions, history, traditions, art, and land; and 
 
WHEREAS, the month of November is a time to celebrate the rich and diverse cultures, to 
raise awareness about our shared history, and to acknowledge the important contributions of 
our Native Heritage; and  
 
WHEREAS, the history and culture of Navajo County has been significantly influenced by 
Native Americans, and by its many surrounding Native American tribes whose customs and 
traditions are respected and celebrated as part of a rich legacy throughout our area; and 
 
WHEREAS, Navajo County was built upon Native American lands and our county has 
greatly benefited since its founding from Native American contributions; and 
 
WHEREAS, we honor all tribes across the nation, including our regions Hopi Nation, 
Navajo Nation and White Mountain Apache Tribe; and  
 
WHEREAS, in celebration of National Native American Heritage Month, Navajo County 
wishes to encourage everyone to join in recognition of the accomplishments and 
contributions the Native American community has made to our society and salute all the 
local organizations who work with and in support of the Native American community. 
 
NOW, THEREFORE , the Navajo County Board of Supervisors, do hereby proclaim 
November 2023 as “NATIONAL NATIVE AMERICAN HERITAGE MONTH.” 
 
Dated this 14th day of November 2023. 
 
       _______________________________ 
       Alberto Peshlakai, Chairman

________________________________

for Excellence in Financial Reporting and an Award of Financial Report Achievement.
Background: 
The Government Finance Officers Association notified the Navajo County Finance Team that
the annual comprehensive financial report for the fiscal year that ended June 30, 2022 qualifies
for GFOA's Certificate of Achievement for Excellence in Financial Reporting.  The Certificate
of Achievement is the highest form of recognition in governmental accounting and financial
reporting, and its attainment represents a significant accomplishment by a government and
its management.
When a Certificate of Achievement is awarded to a government, an Award of Financial
Reporting Achievement (AFRA) is also presented to the individual(s) or department designated
by the government as primarily responsible for its having earned the Certificate.

Board of Supervisors Regular 5. a.        
Meeting Date: 11/14/2023  
Title: AZ DEMA Border Security Fund Award
Submitted For: David Clouse, Sheriff 
Submitted By: Kimberley Willis, Sheriff's Office Finance Manager
Department: Sheriff 
Presented By: Sheriff David M. Clouse
Motion before the Board:
Consideration and approval of new funds awarded to the Navajo County Sheriff's Office by the
Arizona Department of Emergency and Military Affairs. 
Background:
The Navajo County Sheriff's Office was invited to participate in a funding opportunity back in
October, 2022 through AZ DEMA. This funding is focused on border, immigration, and
smuggling issues that are impacting our area. Funding was applied for by the Sheriff's Office
for both Prosecution and Imprisonment (HB 2862) and Border Technology (HB 2317),
The Prosecution and Imprisonment funding will pay partial salary and ERE for 3 employees,
including the Booking Coordinator, Office Support Specialist, and K9 Detention Deputy.
Additionally, equipment consisting of a Lucas Chest Compression System, an AED machine,
and partial funding for a new Ford ADA compliant jail transport was pursued. Finally,
reimbursed costs associated with housing expenses and jail medical expenses for border/drug
related incarcerations were included in the proposal. The total amount awarded for this project is
$3,005,493.00. 
For the Border Technology funding, the Office applied for funding for 175 each of mobile and
portable radios, radio tower equipment for 8 sites, associated additional costs for interoperability
in Navajo County, a rapid deployable cell tower, mapping software, emergency medical
dispatching software, and finally operational and overtime costs associated with the Major
Crimes Apprehension Team. The total amount awarded for this project is $4,130,860.00. 
The effective date for this funding is retro-active from October 1, 2022 through September 30,
2027.
 
Recommendation: 
The Navajo County Sheriff's Office recommends acceptance and approval of grant funding
totaling $7,136,353.00 over a 5 year time span.

1. Recitals: The purpose of this Agreement is to define the terms under which DEMA will provide funds to the County for 
equipment and/or activities related to the prosecution and imprisonment of individuals charged with drug trafficking, human 
smuggling, illegal immigration, and other border-related crimes, and that comply with Section 26-105 Arizona Revised Statutes, 
conducted by the County to be reimbursed by DEMA.  
2. Definitions: The Parties agree to expeditiously initiate and complete the Scope of Work under this Agreement. The Parties 
warrant, represent and agree that they, their employees, and representatives wil l comply with all applicable provisions provided 
herein. The following definitions shall apply to the terms used in this Agreement, except where the context necessarily requi res 
otherwise.  
2.1. “A.R.S.” means Arizona Revised Statutes.  
 
2.2. “Agreement” means the terms and conditions of this Agreement between the State of Arizona Department of Emergency 
Management and Military Affairs (STATE) and Navajo County and the Navajo County Sheriff’s Office together (The County), 
and its addendums: Scope of Work, (Addendum A), Price Sheet (Addendum B), and Budget and Justification (Addendum C), 
constitute the entire Agreement between the Parties and supersede other understandings, oral or written.   
2.3. “County” means the Navajo County and the Navajo County Sheriff’s Office  together, unless context requires that they be 
treated as separate entities. Unless treated as separate entities, Navajo County and the Navajo County Sheriff’s Office  shall be 
treated as a single Party to this Agreement, and shall jointly have, exercise, and be responsible for the same rights and obligations 
under this Agreement. 
2.4 “FY” means State Fiscal Year.  
2.5. “Party” and/or "Parties” means DEMA and/or the Navajo County.  
2.6. “Project” means activities conducted within Scope of Work and from Border Security funds.   
2.7. “State” means the State of Arizona.  
3. Access to Information: Subject to statutory confidentiality requirements of the State of Arizona, the Parties to this Agreement 
shall have full, complete, and equal access to data and information prepared under this Agreement on a no -charge basis.  
4. Amendment: This Agreement, excluding Addendums, may be modified only by written Amendment signed and dated by 
authorized representatives of each signatory (treating the Navajo County and the Navajo County Sheriff’s Office  as separate 
signatories for this purpose) to this Agreement. Amendments to this Agreement shall be executed with the same form alities as 
this Agreement and become effective upon the dated  signature of the last signatory (again, treating the Navajo County and the 
Navajo County Sheriff’s Office  as separate signatories for this purpose). Executed copies of any Amendment shall be provided 
to each signatory.  
4.1. Addendum Amendments: Addendums to this Agreement may be amended or modified, as necessary, only by the Parties’ 
authorized contracting and procurement officers.

JUSTIFICATION: 
 
Booking Coordinator:  The Navajo County Sheriff's Office employs one dedicated coordinator that supervises 
all persons entering the Jail facility at intake.  This employee monitors the charges of all bookings to include 
drug possession charges and drug smuggling cases.  This employee maintains and audits the records of drug 
related charges and prepares reports to the Command Staff at the Sh eriff’s Office and the Jail.  This employee 
ensures quality assurance for all bookings into the jail and tracks all fentanyl overdoses and emergency de -tox.  
The Sheriff’s Office proposes this staff member’s salary be 50% funding through DEMA.  
 
Office Support Specialist:  The Navajo County Sheriff's Office employs an office specialist that fields calls from 
the prosecution, defense, families, bondsmen, etc.  This employee enters and tracks all ICE detainees and ICE 
holds through the jail records management system, scans and enters all court documentation in relation to each 
inmate, audits court dates to follow through the judicial system.  The Sheriff’s Office proposes this staff 
member’s salary be 50% funded through DEMA.

K9 Detention Deputy:  Approximately one year ago the Sheriff’s Office implemented a K9 program in the Jail.  
The handler is a Detention Deputy and is primarily assigned to the Jail Facility conducting cell searches.  The 
Detention Deputy is equipped with a K9 police vehicle and is available to respond to conduct roadside sniffs.  
The Jail is approximately ½ mile away from Interstate 40 which makes a quick response to assist drug 
interdiction efforts.  The main purpose supporting our decision to implement a K9 in the jail was due to an 
alarming increase of fentanyl being smuggled into the jail facility.  The Jail purchased and installed a body 
scanner and implemented a K9 program to deter the introduction of any drugs, specifically fentanyl.  We have 
experienced a dramatic decrease of drugs i nside the jail facility since.   The Sheriff’s Office is proposing the 
Detention K9 Deputy salary is funded 50% through DEMA.

JUSTIFICATION: 
Lucas Chest Compression System:  The NCSO Jail has a 420-bed detention facility that maintains approximately 
300 inmates daily.  The detention facility provides in- custody housing for all State and Local LE Agencies in the 
County as well as contract custody with the US Bureau of Indian Affairs and US Marshall’s Office for ICE Detainees.  
The Jail has experienced a severe increase in persons entering intake that are under the influence of CNS Stimulants 
and Narcotic Analgesics, specifically Fentanyl.  The detainees regularly experience overdos e conditions and de -
toxification.  The chest compression system will enhance staff’s ability to provide life saving measures until the 
arrival of EMS. 
2020 ADA Compliant Transport Van:  The Navajo County Jail currently has four transport vans and one SUV 
vehicle designated for prisoner transport.  None of the vehicles are compliant with Americans with Disability Act 
(ADA) regulations.  The Jail intends on reducing the transport van fleet to one van, one ADA compliant van and one 
SUV, reducing the fleet by two.

JUSTIFICATION: 
 
 The Navajo County Sheriff's Office utilizes a daily matrix of $105.00 per day to house inmates.  This matrix 
consists of combined costs to include staff, utilities, food, laundry, transportation, medical, medical provider 
contracts, mental health contracts, maintenance, and security measures to mention a few.  The staff have recognized 
an increase that is consistent with all other aspects of statistical increases related to Fentanyl and other drugs that are 
100% smuggled from across the southern international border.  These statistics are non -citizen individuals arrested 
for possession of dangerous drugs or narcotic drugs for sale and/or transportation of dangerous drugs or narcotic 
drugs.   
 
 Navajo County Jail Housing and Medical Expenses:  The Navajo County Sheriff’s Office has recognized a 
37% increase in calls for service relating to drug overdoses, specifically relating to Fentanyl.  The Jail has experienced 
a 53% increase in de- tox cases that occur during the intake process or while being housed at the  facility.  The Jail 
Medical Unit has also seen a progressive increase in medical transports from the jail to a medical facility as a result 
of overdose and detox cases with a 31% increase from fiscal year 2020 -2021 to 2021-2022.  These increases create 
a significant drain on the staffing and medical budgeting.  The responsibility of the transport and hospitalization costs 
fall onto the county and the taxpayers of Navajo County as the State suspends DES support when a person is 
incarcerated. 
 
 The Sheriff’s Office is requesting $412,650.00 annually to off-set anticipated costs based on previous year’s 
calculation for border related booking and housing costs.  The continuing influx of unlawful drugs being smuggled

into United States, landing in communities th roughout the State of Arizona, is extremely taxing on the budgets of 
small communities and counties.  This problem is not anticipated to improve. 
 
 The Sheriff’s Office has expended $75,336.00 in calendar year 2021 for medical transports and 
hospitalization directly relating to emergency de -tox and overdose events from the jail.  This amount only is the 
amount that has been invoiced from a medical transport service or medical facility, it does not include the staffing 
expense for a Detention Deputy’s overtime. 
 
 There were 24 deaths in Navajo County attributed to an overdose of either a single drug or a combination 
of drugs in 2021.  Sixteen of those were confirmed Fentanyl overdose cases.  Most of the deaths were classified as 
accidents (92%).  Again, as Arizona serves as a major trans-shipment zone for the Sinaloa Cartel and other Mexican 
DTOs, the increased production of Fentanyl in Mexico correlates to a higher number of Fentanyl Seizures in Arizona.

Meeting Date: 11/14/2023  
Title: Update Delegation Agreement AGR2017-050 to ARG2023-030 Arizona
Department of Health Services
Submitted For: Janelle Linn, Health Director 
Submitted By: Kathryn Mathewson, Environmental Health Program Manager
Department: NC Public Health Services District Division: Code Enforcement Division
Motion before the Board:
Delegation Agreement AGR2023-030 Between the Arizona Department of Health Services and
Navajo County
Background:
The Arizona Department of Health Services (“ADHS”) is authorized by A.R.S. § 36-601.01(G)(10) to
delegate to a political subdivision of this state any functions, powers or duties under the Smoke-Free
Arizona Act.  ADHS is authorized by A.R.S. § 36-136(E) to delegate to a local health department, county
environmental department, or public health services district any functions, powers, or duties that the
ADHS Director (“Director”) believes can be competently, efficiently, and properly performed by the local
health department, county environmental department, or public health services district. 
Therefore, the Director delegates to the County, and the County agrees to accept and perform the
functions, powers, and duties described in Appendix B, in accordance with the terms and conditions of
this Agreement thus amended. The functions, powers, and duties to be retained by ADHS are described
in Appendix B.

DELEGATION AGREEMENT 
 
between 
 
ARIZONA DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH SERVICES 
 
and 
 
NAVAJO COUNTY 
 
A Delegation Agreement is defined in Arizona Revised Statutes (“A.R.S.”) § 41 -1001(8) as “an agreement between 
an agency and a political subdivision that authorizes the political subdivision to exercise functions, powers and duties 
conferred on the delegating agency by a provision of law.” A.R.S. § 41 -1081 establishes standards of delegation. 
  
The Arizona Department of Health Services ( “ADHS”) is authorized by A.R.S. § 36 -601.01(G)(10) to delegate to a 
political subdivision of this state any functions, powers or duties under the Smoke -Free Arizona Act.  ADHS is 
authorized by A.R.S. § 36-136(E) to delegate to a local health department, county environmental department, or public 
health services district any functions, powers, or duties that the ADHS Director (“Director”) believes can be 
competently, efficiently, and properly performed by the local health department, county environmental department, or 
public health services district. 
 
Navajo County ( "County") is a political subdivision of this state. See A.R.S. §§ 11 -111 and 38 -382. As a political 
subdivision of this state, Navajo County, through its County Public Health Services District, may carry out delegated 
functions, powers, and duties on behalf of ADHS. See A.R.S. §§ 36 -136(E), 36 -182, 36 -601.01(G)(10) and 41 -
1001(8). 
 
A.R.S. § 11-201(A)(3) authorizes the Navajo County Board of Supervisors to enter into contracts as necessary to assist 
the County in exercising its powers. 
 
This Amendment (“Amendment”) revises and replaces Delegation Agreement Number AGR20 23-030, as amended 
(“Agreement”) in its entirety.  All terms and conditions of this Amendment shall supersede all prior terms and 
conditions of the Agreement. All references to “Agreement” herein after in this Amendment shall mean the terms and 
conditions of this Amendment. 
 
Therefore, the Director delegates to the County, and the County agrees to accept and perform the functions, powers, 
and duties described in Appendix B, in accordance with the terms and conditions of this Agreement thus amended. 
The functions, powers, and duties to be retained by ADHS are described in Appendix B. 
 
1. RECORDS AND INSPECTIONS: 
 
1.1. The County agrees to retain all records and data related to the delegated functions, powers, and 
duties identified in Appendix B. 
 
1.2. The County agrees to retain all records and data according to the Arizona State Library, Archives 
and Public Records, General Records Retention Schedule for All State and Local Agencies for 
Environmental Quality, Health, Management and Sustainability Recor ds. See 
http://apps.azlibrary.gov/records/general.aspx for more information. 
 
1.3. All records are subject to inspection and audit by the ADHS’ Office of Food Safety and 
Environmental Services (“OFSES”). Upon receiving a request for records from OFSES, the County 
agrees to produce a legible copy of any or all such records as requested to OFSES within five (5) 
business days of receiving the OFSES records request. 
 
1.4. An OFSES representative, after providing prior notice to the County, may accompany County

<!-- page 635 -->
DELEGATION AGREEMENT 
No. AGR2023-030 
AMENDMENT 
Page 2 of 12 
 
representatives on inspections related to delegated functions and review all County records related 
to delegated functions, powers, and duties identified in Appendix B. 
 
1.5. A County representative, after providing prior notice to OFSES, may request to accompany an 
OFSES representative on an OFSES inspection for the purposes of training, information sharing, or 
to coordinate County and OFSES actions related to delegated functions, powers, and duties 
identified in Appendix B. 
 
2. ENFORCEMENT ACTIONS: 
 
2.1. The County, when exercising enforcement related to delegated functions, powers, and duties under 
this Agreement, shall comply with all applicable state statutes and rules identified in Appendix B. 
 
2.2. The County shall be responsible for enforcement actions for those functions, powers, and duties 
identified in Appendix B. 
 
2.3. The County shall respond to public nuisances dangerous to public health, as specified in  A.R.S. § 
36-601(A), and which falls under the County's delegated functions, powers, and duties identified in 
Appendix B. The OFSES retains the authority to also respond to public nuisances dangerous to the 
public health. Unless a public nuisance dangerous to public health exists, no enforcement actions 
on a delegated function will be initiated by the OFSES until the County has received notice of a 
violation from OFSES and the County has had five (5) business days after receipt of the OFSES 
notice of violation to initiate an enforcement action. 
 
2.4. The County shall be responsible for the following: 
 
2.4.1. Food Safety and General Sanitation Control: 
 
See Appendix B. 
 
2.4.2. Pure Food Control: 
 
According to delegated functions, powers, and duties in Appendix B, the County shall 
administer and enforce the provisions of A.R.S. §§ 36 -901 through 36 -916 which 
prohibits the manufacture, sale, holdings or delivery of adulterated and misbranded 
foods.  Where adulterated or misbranded food is manufactured, sold, held, or delivered 
from or within the County, and no portion of such manufacture sale, holding, or 
delivery occurs within any other county of the state, the County may take enforcement 
action with out first notifying OFSES. However, if any portion of the manufacture, 
sale, delivery, holding, or offering for sale of adulterated or misbranded food occurs 
within any other county of the state, the County shall notify OFSES of a notice of 
violation and h as five (5) business days from the date the notice was received. The 
County shall, within 24 hours of identifying an emergency case, provide notice of 
violation to the OFSES of the nature and extent of the violation of state statutes or 
rules relating to a dulterated or misbranded foods, and shall provide additional 
information as OFSES may require. See Appendix B. 
 
2.4.3. Smoke-Free Arizona Act: 
 
County shall be responsible for the education, inspections, investigations, complaint 
responses and appropriate enforcement actions for the Smoke -Free Arizona Act 
according to delegated functions, powers, and duties identified in Appendix B.

3. FEES AND CIVIL PENALTIES: 
 
The County is authorized to collect fees and assess civil penalties by: A.R.S. §§ 36 -183.04; 36-183.05; 36-
187; and 36 -602. The County is also authorized to collect fees and assess civil penalties for delegated 
functions, powers, and duties under this Agre ement, if such authority is included in the laws and rules 
identified in Appendix B. 
 
4. QUALIFICATIONS OF PERSONNEL: 
 
4.1. A County representative exercising delegated functions, powers, and duties identified in Appendix 
B with regard to Food and General Sanitation Control and Pure Food Control shall be an Arizona 
Registered Sanitarian authorized by A.R.S. § 36 -136.01 or an unregistered individual that prepares 
and submits inspection reports to an Arizona Registered Sanitarian. Individuals that are not 
registered sanitarians shall not approve or disapprove the operation of a food establishment.  
 
4.2. A County representative exercising delegated functions, powers, and duties identified in Appendix 
B with regard to the Smoke-Free Arizona Act, shall meet County personnel rules. 
 
5. STANDARDS OF PERFORMANCE AND REPORTING: 
 
5.1. The County’s performance of delegated functions under the Agreement shall be in accordance with 
state statutes and rules identified in Appendix B and inspections for: 
 
5.1.1. Food establishments shall be inspected at a frequency outlined in Arizona 
Administrative Code (“A.A.C.”) Title 9, Chapter 8, Article 1. 
 
5.1.2. Semi-public bathing places shall be inspected at least once each calendar year and 
public swimming pools shall be inspected at least once for every 30 days the public 
swimming pool is open for public use. 
 
5.1.3. Public schools shall be inspected at least once each calendar year. 
 
5.2. Unregistered individuals conducting food safety inspections shall receive training on A.A.C. Title 
9, Chapter 8, Article 1 or have completed the Food and Drug Administration's Voluntary National 
Retail Food Regulatory Program Standards Standard 2 prerequisite training curriculum prior to 
conducting independent retail food inspections. 
 
5.3. The County shall provide annually a: 
 
5.3.1. Food and General Sanitation Annual Report to the OFSES Food Safety & 
Environmental Services Section, using the form provided in Appendix C, by 
September 1; and 
 
5.3.2. Smoke-Free Arizona Annual Report to the OFSES Smoke-Free Arizona Section, using 
the form provided in Appendix D, by May 10. 
 
6. TERMINATION: 
 
6.1. This Agreement may be terminated in whole or in part by the Director or the County, effective 
ninety (90) calendar days after either the Director or the County provides written notice of 
termination by certified mail to the other. 
 
6.2. The County, prior to the termination of all or part of this Agreement, shall forward to the Director:

6.2.1. A list and summary of the functions, powers, and duties the County is terminating;  
 
6.2.2. All pending complaints and enforcement actions received by the County for those 
functions, powers, and duties being terminated; 
 
6.2.3. The Smoke-Free Arizona Annual Report, identified in Appendix D, updated from the 
date of the last Smoke-Free Arizona Annual Report submitted to ADHS for analyzing 
Smoke-Free Arizona activities to enforce this law, including all complaints and 
education outreach and enforcement activities by the County; 
 
6.2.4. A list of names of the persons and regulated facilities affected by the termination and 
to whom notification of termination was sent; and 
 
6.2.5. All records retained according to subsection 1.2. 
 
6.3. The provisions of A.R.S. § 38-511 are incorporated herein by reference. 
 
7. AMENDMENTS: 
 
This Agreement may be amended by mutual approval of both the Director and the County by executing and 
filing a written amendment signed by both the Director and the County containing the desired modifications 
as required in A.R.S. § 41-1081. 
 
8. DISPUTES: 
 
8.1. Pursuant to A.R.S. § 12 -1518, the Director and the County agree to use arbitration specified in 
A.R.S. § 12 -133, should a dispute under this Agreement occur which cannot be resolved by the 
Director and the County. 
 
8.2. In the event of a dispute between the Director and the County under this Agreement, the OFSES or 
the County with who a matter in dispute is claimed will: 
 
8.2.1. Provide to the other a written notice of the matter in dispute and intent to resolve the 
matter in dispute, including a notice of proposed meeting to discuss and resolve the 
matter in dispute. 
 
8.2.2. After the meeting to resolve the matter in dispute, the OFSES and County will 
implement the resolution agreed to by the OFSES and the County within 10 business 
day of the date -of-the-meeting; unless during the meeting, the OFSES and County 
agreed to extend the period needed for resolution. 
 
8.2.3. If after the meeting, a resolution is not reached between the OFSES and the County, 
the matter in dispute shall be resolved through the use of arbitration as stated in 
subsection 8.3. 
 
8.3. In the event that the dispute between the Director and the County identified in subsection 8.2 is not 
resolved, the Director or the County with who a matter in dispute is claimed, shall provide to the 
other notice of intent to seek resolution through arbitration. The Director or the County with who a 
matter in dispute is claimed shall proceed with arbitration as specified in A.R.S. § 12-133.

Board of Supervisors Regular 6. b. 1.        
Meeting Date: 11/14/2023  
Title: Arizona Mutual Aid Compact
Submitted For: Catrina Jenkins, EMP Director 
Submitted By: Catrina Jenkins, EMP Director
Department: NC Public Health Services District Division: Emergency Management
Presented By: Catrina Jenkins
Motion before the Board:
Consideration of the adoption of Resolution Number 44-2023, approving and authorizing the
Chairperson to execute the revised Arizona Mutual Aid Compact (AZMAC) for Emergency
Mutual Aid.  
Background:
In 2014 Navajo County signed on to the Arizona Mutual Aid Compact which has been modified
to provide clarification on several key points. The AZMAC enables participating agencies to
share resources, personnel, etc. during emergencies and then be reimbursed for the resources.
The agreement will provide means for participants to quickly obtain emergency assistance
through a centralized method. The agreement provides means and methods for agencies
providing assistance for requesting reimbursements to requesting agencies as outlined in the
agreement.  The previous agreement will expire December 31, 2023 at midnight and the new
agreement will take effect January 1, 2024 and will last for 10 years. NCEM will be working
with all political subdivisions and tax levying public districts to sign on to the compact if they
are interested in this agreement. 
Recommendation: 
Staff recommends approval.

RESOLUTION ____-23 
 
A RESOLUTION OF THE NAVAJO COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS, 
APPROVING AND AUTHORIZING THE CHAIRMAN TO EXECUTE THE REVISED 
“ARIZONA MUTUAL AID COMPACT (AZMAC)” FOR EMERGENCY MUTUAL AID 
 
WHEREAS, one or more Parties may find it necessary to utilize all their own resources to cope 
with emergencies, and may require the assistance of another Party or other Parties; and  
 
WHEREAS, it is desirable that all resources of all Parties be available to all other Parties on 
preestablished terms, in order to respond to such emergencies; and 
 
WHEREAS, it is desirable that each of the Parties should assist one another when such 
emergency occurs by providing such resources as are available and needed, including, but not 
limited to, fire, police, medical and health, environmental, communication, and transportation 
services to cope with the problems of response; and 
 
WHEREAS, it is desirable that a compact be executed for the interchange of such mutual aid; 
and 
 
WHEREAS, it is desirable to utilize this Compact in exercising adopted emergency plans; and 
  
WHEREAS, it is desirable that the manner of financing of such cooperative undertakings be 
resolved in advance of such emergency. 
 
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the Navajo County Board of Supervisors that the 
Chairman is hereby authorized to execute on behalf of Navajo County, the Arizona mutual aid 
compact in the form attached hereto and that such agreement shall be deemed effective as of 
January 1, 2024.  
 
PASSED, ADOPTED AND APPROVED by the Navajo County Board of Supervisors on this 
14th day of November 2023.  
 
 
 NAVAJO COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS
