Neighborhood Meeting Notice—7/27 6:00-8:00PM @ WMLE 
Community Center—1785 Edmonds Circle 
 
FOR 
 
Vertical Bridge US-AZ-5117 Silver Creek  
80’ Multi-Carrier Communications Pole 
 
1785 Edmonds Circle 
Show Low, AZ 85901 
APN: 304-34-328 
Jurisdiction:  Navajo County 
Zoning:  R1-10 
 
Yellow Pins denote existing Verizon sites.  Proposed Vertical Bridge site is Green Pin 
 
Submitted by: 
Reg Destree 
Destree Development, LLC 
22831 N. 21st St 
Phoenix, AZ 85024 
602-349-6930 (mobile) 
destreedevelopment@gmail.com 
July 9, 2023

<!-- page 855 -->
Purpose of Notice 
 Vertical Bridge Communications is proposing to place a new 80’ multi-carrier Wireless Facility 
(Monopole) on the Community Center property at 1785 Edmonds Circle.  As part of the Citizen 
Participation process I will be holding a neighborhood meeting July 27th  from 6:00-8:00PM at the 
Community Center. 
 
 You are receiving this notice as you own property within 300’ of the subject parcel at 1785 
Edmonds Circle. 
 
 If you are unable to attend but would like further information, feel free to reach out to me with any 
questions or comments.   
 
Purpose of Application 
 
As part of its ongoing effort to maintain the pre-eminent wireless network in Navajo County, 
Verizon Wireless has engaged Vertical Bridge to develop several sites within the County to improve 
coverage and capacity for Verizon’s network.  This approach is being used to allow for the County to be 
built out faster than if Verizon was developing the sites directly.  Vertical Bridge is one of a few companies 
who have been engaged for different locations throughout the County as part of an overall development 
plan meant to improve rural broadband and overall connectivity.  Vertical Bridge is a large tower 
development and management firm with sites throughout the country and many within Arizona.   
 
This proposal is for a new site in the White Mountain Lake Estates neighborhood.  This site is 
meant to work in conjunction with the existing site to the west at Juniper Ridge.  As I stated when we went 
through the Special Use Permit process for the pole at Juniper Ridge, there would likely need to be a new 
site a few miles east to provide in-building coverage to folks in the eastern part of this development.  That 
is what we are now proposing.   
 
This site is meant to ensure good in-building coverage in this area as well as offer some 
improvement heading north and south along Bourdon Ranch Road.  White Mountain Lakes Estates has 
coverage which drops off quickly on its eastern side as it is currently served by the site at Juniper Ridge.  
Verizon has requested this site to become the primary serving site for the area.  This site will have a 
secondary benefit of offloading capacity at Juniper Ridge which should improve the performance of that 
site for the folks at Juniper Ridge.  It also will integrate with a future site which will be along Bourdon Ranch 
north of the Airport.   
 
While the anchor tenant will be Verizon Wireless, the structure is being developed to handle 
additional carriers if they choose to use it in the future.  Smith Bagley does have a tower a bit over a mile 
west of this location so they would not likely need to collocate but there are two other carriers operating in 
this market. 
 
The primary focus for coverage and capacity was in more densely populated areas and along 
major thoroughfares within the last 5-10 years.  As areas such as this have become more populated and 
technologies have advanced, it is becoming necessary to build additional structures to accommodate 
coverage for residents, visitors and travelers in these areas.  This is a pretty dense area with homes on 
small lots.  Capacity is an issue on the west side of White Mountain Lakes Estates and coverage is an 
issue in the homes on the east side.  This site will help with both of those problems. 
 
 Due to the size and location of the pole at Juniper Ridge it can’t effectively service this area.  The 
existing tower owned by CellOne at the Fire Station is in a spot which makes it a poor option for 
collocation.  It is too close to Juniper Ridge and would overpower that site and is still too far from the east 
side of White Mountain Estates to provide the in-building coverage we need from this site.  As noted 
above, this was actually discussed when Juniper Ridge went through the zoning process.  The plan has 
always been to place multiple sites in this area.

<!-- page 856 -->
Vertical Bridge is requesting a Special Use Permit for a 80’ tall multi-carrier wireless monopole 
within a 50’ x 50’ compound.  There will be ground equipment within the compound.  The height has been 
reduced from the previously proposed 99’ to adhere to the new Wireless Ordinance.       
 
Site Description 
 
The subject parcel is just over 2.5 acres and is surrounded entirely by Edmonds Circle with homes 
on the parcels on the outside of the circle.  This parcel is owned by the Association and used for the 
Community Center/Library as well as the US Post Office.  The Parcel is zoned R1-10 but is one of the few 
non-residential uses in the development.  It is also one of the largest parcels in the development.     
 
The compound will be just east and southeast of the existing building with the community Center 
and the Post office.  This was done to cluster it with the existing buildings yet put it a reasonable distance 
from the surrounding road and homes beyond.  The location allows the pole to be about as far from 
neighboring homes as possible in this community and it is close to the center of the parcel as we could get.    
 
Site History 
 
Verizon Wireless has been working on improving coverage in Navajo County for many years.  That 
often involves a few sites every year.  Now that 5G is being deployed to provide rural broadband coverage 
throughout much of Navajo County, Verizon has a need for several sit es within the next year or two.  
Verizon approached several tower developers about different sites throughout the County.  Vertical Bridge 
is one of the two main tower developers and current ly is loo king at this site.   The east side of this 
community is a targeted location requested by Verizon.   
 
As noted above, Verizon previously developed a site at Juniper Ridge two miles to the west.  It was 
always expected future sites would be needed, especially as technology advanced.  The original proposed 
location for this ring by the carrier was further east , near Bourdon Ranch Road.   Unfortunately , there is 
very little private land in that area, the parcels are very small and there would likely be issues  with the 
airstrip.    When I spoke with the en gineer to determine the desired c overage it became cl ear that this 
location would work to achieve the objectives but we couldn’ t really move any further west as it would 
begin encroaching on and overlapping the site at Juniper Ridge.   
 
I began looking at property records and noticed this parcel was owned by the Association.  It was a 
logical choice as a non- residential use and it also gives you, the neighbors,  an additional opportunity to 
provide feedback on the design.  I devel oped a proposal for the location to keep the pole as far from your  
homes across the circle as reasonably possibl e.  Vertical Bridge entered into a Lease agreement with the 
Association and we are now moving forward with the entitlement process. 
 
Description of Proposal 
 
The proposed site development includes placement of panel antennas on a new 80’ monopole.  
The panel antennas are used for coverage to communicate with phones and other devices.  The 80’ is 
meant to provide a site which meets the needs of Verizon but also leaves space for one to two carriers to 
collocate in the future.  Verizon’s antennas will be at 76’ on the pole to maximize integration with the site at 
Juniper Ridge and the future site north of the Airport.  The pole will be structurally capable of handling 
additional carriers and have usable space available within the compound.   
 
The proposed location is about as close as we could get to the center of the Association’s 2.5 acre 
parcel.  It is more than 1:1 from all property lines and the parcel is surrounded entirely by Edmonds Circle.  
There is currently one home within 200’ of the pole location to the south and a total of 10 homes within 
400’ of the proposed site.  There aren’t other locations within this development which would be able to

<!-- page 857 -->
keep the site further from homes.  The location also is close to commercial power and appears to have 
fiber service available.  Access will come from the Edmonds Circle through the existing parking lot.   
 
The 50’ x 50’ compound is located just ESE of the existing building.  The pole is in the center of the 
compound.  The pole exceeds a 1:1 setback from all property lines. 
   
The Verizon radio equipment will be on a small outdoor platform.  The site will have an emergency 
back-up generator.  The site has commercial power which will come from the existing power pole just SW 
of the main building on the property.   
 
The site will take about 60-90 days to construct, and once complete, will be visited approximately 
once per month for maintenance.  This development is unoccupied and does not involve water or sewer.  
There will not be any changes to existing watercourses or an impact on off-site discharge of rainwater.     
   
 
 
 
Citizen Participation Plan 
 
As previously noted, this site has already been considered and approved by the White Mountain 
Lakes Estates Association.  This was discussed at a Board meeting prior to approval and has been 
discussed further at meetings since the original approval. 
 
This meeting is meant to give you an additional opportunity to provide feedback and be involved in 
the proposed design as a neighborhood stakeholder.  A report of this meeting will be provided to County 
staff.  In addition to this meeting the site will require Public Hearings with Navajo County.  The time(s) and 
date(s) of the County meetings are TBD. 
 
Conclusion 
 
This type of facility requires a Special Use Permit in Navajo County.  This proposal meets the intent 
of the new Wireless Ordinance.  Vertical Bridge will be requesting a Special Use Permit for this proposed 
site for the maximum length of time available.  This site will benefit many of you as well as visitors and 
travelers in this area.

Neighborhood Meeting Report 
 
FOR 
 
Vertical Bridge US-AZ-5117 Silver Creek  
80’ Multi-Carrier Communications Pole 
 
1785 Edmonds Circle 
Show Low, AZ 85901 
APN: 304-34-328 
Jurisdiction:  Navajo County 
Zoning:  R1-10 
 
Notices were sent to the neighborhood via USPS on July 8th.   
 
I sent out notices to all neighbors within 300’ of the property.  I have attached a copy of the labels and 
the notice letter to this Report.  I have also attached the sign-in sheets I got from the meeting 
including names and feedback on the site. 
  
Feedback prior to meeting from Notice:  
I did not receive any direct questions beyond what was raised previously during Community 
Association meetings where this site was discussed several times, including the meeting many 
months ago when they signed the Lease for this site.  I did provide information as to why this site was 
selected, why the existing CellOne Tower wouldn’t work and why we weren’t proposing the site 
outside of this area. 
 
I did join the Community Facebook page in case there was any discussion regarding the site.  There 
were some regular posts about it, primarily they related to health concerns.  There were some people 
in favor of the site on these strings regarding health concerns and a majority opposed to the site 
based on this. 
 
Meeting Notes:  
 
On 7/27 I Arrived at 5:46 and set up.  The meeting room was already open and there were over a 
dozen attendees, even by the time I arrived.  We asked anyone there to sign in and provide written 
comments that I could include in this report. 
 
The Association was kind enough to set this up as a special Board meeting so the Board members 
could be there and they could live-stream the event.  This allowed us to have folks view remotely and 
even ask several questions.   
 
Shortly after 6 we began, and I introduced myself to the attendees.  I gave a short presentation for 
several minutes just providing basic site information regarding the company, the client and how we 
came to this location and proposed design.  At the beginning of the meeting there were about 30 
people in person and a few on the livestream.

<!-- page 864 -->
From my count there were anywhere from 25-30 people in attendance for the majority of the 
time.  There were 27 people on the sign-in sheet.  I did an informal show of hands up front and about 
20 were opposed, 5 were in favor and 4 were undecided.  When I asked later what the reason for 
opposition was and whether it was 5G basically all 20 opposed raised their hands. 
 
 We got through pretty much all of the questions at about 7:50 and ended the meeting promptly 
at 8.  We did have some in-person discussions after the meeting but nothing particularly different than 
what was discussed as a group. 
 
 
 
Questions from the Audience (not necessarily in the order they were asked and each is only listed 
once) 
 
 Will this site have 5G?  This was the main question of the night.  I did make it clear that this 
site would have 4G and 5G when built and tried to explain that 5G is simply a network standard for 
throughput and I also let them know this site would not have MMWave frequency bands. 
 
 Health concerns/Safety:  This was the primary issue and was related to the 5G note above.  
The majority of those opposed to the site did not feel it was safe to have a 5G transmitter in the 
neighborhood.  There did not seem to be concern from most of them regarding older technology 
standards.  The concerns ranged from issues with 5G activating issues with COVID Vaccines to 
cancer to one attendee who recently got a pacemaker but was concerned how it might impact that.  I 
did also mention setbacks regarding pole height and explained that the site is more than its height 
from all property lines, I also mentioned that we will be requesting relief as we are less than 2:1 but 
we are well beyond a full fall zone to stay on property.  I did point out some of the benefits for safety 
and security of having good coverage, being able to call in case of an emergency and even 
mentioned to the person with the pacemaker how my father’s pacemaker uses Bluetooth to 
communicate to his phone and then back to his Doctor to inform the Doctor of any heart issues it is 
sensing regularly. 
 
 How can they ensure the site is operating within its license/they wanted full information on the 
emissions:  I actually suggested that we could have the County require a Pre and Post-EME study on 
the towers.  There are some cities that require these and carriers are able to provide a version which 
can be given to jurisdictions (Scottsdale requires this on sites). 
 
 Why do we need a site if I already have coverage?  I explained that non-Verizon customers 
would not be benefited unless their carrier joined the site in the future.  Most of the attendees were 
either Verizon customers or CellOne customers.  Most of the Cell One customers do have coverage 
and a some of the Verizon customers to the West also have coverage but more than 5 of the folks 
were Verizon customers in support because they don’t have good service near or east of the 
community center. 
 
 Why this location/Why not CellOne tower?  I explained how I came to this spot based on 
direction from the engineering team to locate in this area.  I explained the standard steps of visiting 
the area, looking for any existing verticality, existing site, power poles, large buildings/structures and 
then looking at raw land sites.  I tried to explain why locating on the CellOne tower a mile west would 
not work due its proximity to the existing site and the technological need for several sites.  I spent 
several minutes explaining why the newer technology requires more sites at lower heights, closer to 
users.  There was also concern about whether I approached the association or they approached me.  
I let the attendees know that I simply approached the association because they had the best parcel 
available due to size, setbacks and use.

<!-- page 865 -->
 Will there be more meetings/How can they stay involved?  I let the group know that we’re 
hoping to have the site built by the middle of next year and then Verizon can locate on it but we still 
will be going through the P&Z, BoS and BP processes, and that is assuming the site is not denied.  I 
let them know there would be notices sent and posted as required by the County and the Association 
will also post anything on their FB page.  I mentioned how the attendance at this meeting 
demonstrated that the word was clearly getting out about this site. 
 
 What will the pole look like/Can we do a tree?  This was a question from one of the online 
attendees.  I let them know that we were initially proposing a standard steel monopole but will now be 
proposing a rusticated pole with brown antennas to cut down on the visual impact.  They asked if we 
could do a tree and I explained that a tree, limited to 80’ to the top of branches limits the height quite a 
bit for the first carrier versus a standard 80’ pole and eliminates at least one future collocator. 
 
 What if someone comes to add antennas/change antennas in the future?  I let them know that 
future collocators would need to go through an Administrative Process with the County but changes in 
antennas for existing users would likely not require that process and there is also the possibility that 
additional frequencies could be added without consulting the County.  I did not get into the fact that 
this is handled at the Federal level and the County is limited on its oversite for these types of 
modifications.  They did also separately indicate that they felt the Federal Government was 
overreaching when this should be a local decision.  That came up several times. 
 
 What if this causes more power outages?  I explained that this site uses a similar power set up 
to a standard home.  The fear was that our additional draw would possibly make a fairly unstable 
system even worse. 
 
 Why can’t alternate means be used?  There were two primary suggestions.  The first was 
giving everyone fiber.  I explained that getting fiber connections to every house in a community is 
extremely expensive and, even once it gets there, it typically goes into a router and over the air from 
there.  The second idea I didn’t quite understand as they kept indicating that “Tesla” has developed a 
system to use the ground to transmit signal.  I let them know I was unfamiliar with this and they 
indicated that they felt industry had buried this option. 
 
 Will the tower owner and carrier have “RFM” insurance?  I had not ever heard of this and 
wasn’t sure what it was.  They indicated it was Radio Frequency Measurement insurance.  I was still 
not sure but let them know that the tower owner and all carriers have standard commercial insurance 
policies on these sites. 
 
 Are we aware of the other proposed sites in the area/why don’t we talk to those folks?  I 
actually mentioned that Verizon had tasked another vendor with placing a site about a mile N or this 
location to cover along Bourdon Ranch Road to the north and cover that part of the community and 
that Verizon was using Vertical Bridge to develop a site several miles SE.  They felt I had not been in 
touch with the other vendors.  I let them know I had not spoken to the vendor from Pinnacle proposing 
the site to the North but I did talk to that company (for whom I also do work) after they had their 
neighborhood meeting.  I also mentioned the site VB is doing to the SE several times and am in 
regular communication with Todd Daoust, who is handling that site.  I did explain that we are doing 
these sites at the behest of Verizon and they have close to 20 sites under development in Navajo and 
Apache Counties.  I let them know these developments are done as part of an overall plan and that is 
why these three sites are located where they are. 
 
 How far do these sites cover?  This question flowed from a few others and I let them know that 
a 65’ site in a flat area with the amount of users/density this area has would typically be the primary

<!-- page 866 -->
server for about 1-1.5 miles and the sites would usually be set up to overlap a bit so the network can 
react to spikes in traffic.  This segued into why this site is 2 miles from the current site, why the 
CellOne tower one mile away and between those two sites won’t work and why there is another 
shorter site to the north and a taller site to the SE.  I also mentioned the site we have called Antelope 
which is about 4 miles SSW of this site.  I did have a coverage map showing sites on air and the 
proposed site (it didn’t show the other two proposed sites yet though) 
 
 There was also a question regarding the contract/terms/process for approval:  I let them know 
I wasn’t sure off the top of my head the contract terms and the Board offered to share the info with 
them.  It was also pointed out that the Board approved and signed the agreement about several 
months ago and this site had been discussed prior to signature and a few times at association 
meetings since.

A RESOLUTION OF THE NAVAJO COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS APPROVING 
A SPECIAL USE PERMIT FOR US-AZ-5117 SILVER CREEK WIRELESS 
COMMUNICATION FACILITY 
 
WHEREAS, an application for a Special Use Permit was duly filed on March 9th, 2023 
by Reg Destree to allow for the construction of a 62’ rusticated monopole wireless 
communication tower and associated facilit ies on a vacant, 2.50-acre parcel, in the White 
Mountain Lakes area; and 
 
WHEREAS, the application concerns the foll owing real p roperty in Navajo County: 
APN # 304-34-328, Township 11 North, Range 22 East, Section 24 of the Gil a and Salt River 
Base and Meridian; and 
 
WHEREAS, the application was considered by the Navajo County Planning & Zoning 
Commission at a duly noticed public hearing on September 21st, 2023; and 
 
WHEREAS, the Navajo County Bo ard of Supervisors after considering the testimony 
and other evidence presented at t he hearing, as well as the recommendations of Staff, found that 
the Special Use Permit is consistent with the public health, safety and general welfare and should 
be approved subject to the conditions set forth herein; and 
 
NOW, THEREFORE BE IT R ESOLVED the Board of Superviso rs hereby 
approves the Special Use Permit, subject to the following conditions: 
 
1. This Specia l Use Permit shall permit 1 (one) monopole wireless communication 
tower, not to exceed 62 feet in height, and accessory structures necessary for the 
operation of the tower on the subject property. 
 
2. The applicant shall obtain a Building Permit from Navajo C ounty for such tower 
and facilities prior to commencing construction. 
 
3. The applicant shal l meet all State and Federal requirements concerning 
communication towers prior to any building permits being issued. 
 
4. The tower shall be constructed as a monopole, as  indicated in the supplied plans.  
The owner of the tower shall maintain the tower, antennae as necessary.

<!-- page 882 -->
Navajo County - For Official Use Only 
5. A fence of material acceptable to the Planning and Development Services Director shall 
be constructed to enclose the base of the tower and necessary accessory structures.  
 
6. A Geotechnical Report for the Access Easement shall be submitted and approved. 
 
7. The permitted Special Use shall be allowed to occur per the attached/approved site 
plan.  Any expansion or change of the Special Use shall require an a mendment to 
this permit. 
 
8. If the permitted Special Use is not utilized within a twelve (12) month period, from 
the date of Board approval, this permit shall become null and void. 
 
9. Should the operator decide to abandon the use of the tower, they shall notif y 
Navajo County Planning and Development Services that the tower is no longer 
being utilized. 
 
10. If the tower is no longer being utilized, the property owner  and/or applicant shall 
cause, at their expense, the removal of all components of this tower within a  90-
day period. 
 
11. The owner shall provide reasonable cooperation to other public and private users 
who may be interested in collocation on this tower and shall consider such 
collocation upon commercially reasonable terms, unless such collocation is not 
technically feasible. 
 
12. This Special Use Permit shall be personal to the permittee and applicable only to the 
specific use and to the specific property for which it is issued. Upon comp letion and final 
inspection by the Planning and Development Services Directo r (or designee) of any 
authorized structures, signifying that all zoning and site development requirements 
imposed in connection with the permit have been satisfied, the Special Us e Permit shall 
thereafter be transferable and shall run with the land, where upon the maintenance of 
special conditions imposed by the permit, as well as the compliance with other provisions 
of this title, shall be the responsibility of the property owner. 
 
13. This Special Use Permit and the subject site shall be reviewed and inspecte d by Planning 
and Development Staff on the fifth (5 th) anniversary of Board of Supervisors approval 
and every five (5) years thereafter to ensure the site is being utilized as approved and is in 
compliance with all conditions contained herein.  If the subj ect site is found to be out of 
compliance with these conditions, this Special Use Permit and its privileges may be 
revoked.

Coverage vs Capacity
Capacity is providing bandwidth or processing 
capacity to service the customers in the area.
– Areas where large numbers of users are in a specific 
geographic areas
– Areas where users are demanding higher data rates 
for services
– Areas with a large amount of indoor users
Coverage is Providing Service where service 
does not exist, calls drop, or “no service”.
– Areas where sites are farther apart
– Areas where terrain or buildings block signals
– Areas where indoor service is low or nonexistent

<!-- page 920 -->
2023
Ionizing vs Non-Ionizing
There are two (2) types of Energy/Radio Waves
– Ionizing
• These are waves that can effect human DNA
• Examples are:
– Gamma rays
– X-Rays
• This is one of the reasons the nurse steps out of the room and you wear a lead overcoat 
when you get X-Rays at the dentist.
– Non- Ionizing
• These are waves do not effect human DNA
• Examples are:
– Car Radios
– Television 
– Wi-Fi Access points and routers
– Bluetooth headsets
– Cellphones and Smartphones
– Lightbulbs
– Wireless Baby Monitors
– TV remotes
– Absorption of waves is proximity based, the closer you are to the antenna the more non-
ionizing energy is absorbed.  You will absorb 50% of the FCC’s General Public limit with your 
smartphone next to your ear versus less than 10% of the FCC’s General Public limit from the 
antennas when you are standing 20’ away from the proposed tower. 
– The further you walk away from the tower it decreases even more.

<!-- page 921 -->
2023
General Public & Occupational limits
The FCC isolated two (2) groups relative to access around wireless antennas
The first group is called Occupational
– This refers to areas where workers would be allowed (general public cannot access) but the workers would 
not have knowledge about antennas (An example would be an Air Conditioner Repair Technician).  Barriers 
or signage may be needed to alert the worker when close to the antennas.
• Examples are:  
– Rooftop access behind a locked door
– Compound access behind a locked gate
– The FCC determined the safe value and then lowered by a factor of 10 and that is the value the 
wireless carriers use in the studies
– The exposure levels are averaged over 6 minutes
The second group is called General Public
– Uncontrolled access (General Public) 
• This group is for areas with general public access, the public would not have a knowledge of an 
antenna being close to them
• Examples are:
– Sidewalks
– Parks
– Public accessed buildings
– The FCC determined the safe value and then lowered by a factor of 50 and that is the value the 
wireless carriers use in the studies
– The exposure levels are averaged over 30 minutes
Compare the value for a tower which is 10mW to the power of a 
smartphone which is 200mW of power.

<!-- page 922 -->
Power Levels below a tower
• Power levels on the 
ground around the 
tower are much less 
than what is at the 
antennas
• Power on the ground 
adjacent to the tower 
is 1/1000th or 30db 
lower compared to 
what is at the antenna

antenna

Title: MDP-A 23-001 Show Low Mountain Ranch, District III
Submitted For: Sondra Starke, Planner I  Submitted By: Cody Cooper, Planning
Manager
Department: Public Works Division: Planning & Development
Presented By: Cody Cooper
Motion before the Board:
PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration of the adoption of Resolution Number 43-2023, to allow
for a Master Development Plan Amendment from an approved, approximately 508-unit,
single-family residential development with commercial uses to be amended to allow for
recreational vehicles/park models and manufactured homes for a total of 758 units along with
amenities, accessory uses, and commercial uses in the Show Low Mountain Ranch Special
Development within the White Mountain Lakes area. 
Background:
There is an existing, approved Master Development Plan for the project. This MDP was approved and
adopted by the Navajo County Board of Supervisors in 2007 through Resolution 96-07 and allowed for
the 307 acres of subject parcels to be developed out to a maximum of 508 units.
There is currently a water tank and water lines already partially installed, and the sewer has been at least
partially tied in to the first phase of the development with a lift station having been installed and a valve
for pressure having been attempted to be installed.
The Navajo County Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously recommended approval of this
Master Development Plan Amendment request to the Board of Supervisors at the September 21st,
2023, meeting, to include all conditions put forth by Staff.
At the Tuesday, October 24th, 2023, Board of Supervisors Hearing, this item was unanimously tabled,
with the request that the applicant hold a community meeting so as to hear concerns from neighbors
within the vicinity of the project.
On Friday, November 3rd, 2023, the applicant held a community meeting at the White Mountain Lakes
Community Association Building/Post Office.  Notice of this meeting was overnighted by the applicant to
all neighbors listed within three hundred feet (300’) of the proposed project boundary.  This notice was
sent to 66 properties, with 61 total addresses.  This meeting was scheduled from 4:00 p.m. until 5:00
p.m.
At the meeting, there were approximately 65 attendees.  This meeting was scheduled for one hour, but
continued from 4:00 p.m. until 6:00 p.m.  Concerns that were raised, and addressed, as possible, were
the following:
  
Issues with the sanitary company, and how the project would plan to expand usage, with

<!-- page 933 -->
Show Low Mountain Ranch 
Amended Master Development Plan – Project Narrative 
Page 2 
Introduction: 
 
Show Low Mountain Ranch is an approved mixed -use development consisting of  
commercial and residential uses, along with related existing infrastructure, on 
approximately 297.4 acres located along Bourdon Ranch Road, approximately 1-¼ miles 
south of White Mountain Lake Road, in unincorporated Navajo County (the “Property”). 
 
Show Low Mountain Ranch is zoned Special Development, which allows for unique  
mixed-use projects such as this one. A Master Development Plan was approved along  
with the Special Development zoning. 
 
This Project Narrative, accompanying Amended Master Development Plan and related 
materials are provided as part of a request for a Major Amendment to the Master 
Development Plan under the approved Special Development zoning. 
 
 
Overview of Request: 
 
As noted above, Show Low Mountain Ranch is approved as a mixed- use development 
with commercial uses along both side of Bourdon Ranch Road and single -family 
residential lots to the west of Bourdon Ranch Road. A portion of Show Low Mountain  
Ranch was mass -graded and some of the major water and wastewater “back bone” 
infrastructure utilities were completed in the early 2010’s. 
 
The Amended Master Development Plan (Zoning Exhibit) included with this request 
indicates the proposed changes for the 297.4-acre portion of Show Low Mountain Ranch 
that is west of Bourdon Ranch Road only; no changes are proposed for the ~9.5-acre 
portion of Show Low Mountain Ranch that is located to the east of Bourdon Ranch Road 
that includes the existing water and wastewater facilities and is labeled “Approved  
Commercial” and “(Not a part of this request).”  
 
The proposed Amendment would allow for recreational vehicle/park models and  
manufactured/modular homes as either/both “ Park” (common ownership) or as a 
subdivision(s), for a total of 758 units and a density of approximately 2.55 dwelling unit s 
per acre, along with amenities, accessory uses and commercial uses as described within 
this Project Narrative. 
 
The proposed Amendment is  a response to changes in market conditions that have  
occurred since Show Low Mountain Ranch was initially envisioned and approved over 15 
years ago. This request for an Amendment is to allow for the following changes, using the 
Amended Master Development Plan (Zoning Exhibit) included with this application as a 
key to where the proposed changes are to occur, especially those related to the proposed 
Land Use Parcels (“Parcels”):

<!-- page 934 -->
Show Low Mountain Ranch 
Amended Master Development Plan – Project Narrative 
Page 3 
▪  Parcel “A” (Commercial alon g the west side of Bourdon Ranch Road)  on 
approximately 6.8 acres: In addition to the commercial uses that are already approved,

1.0   INTRODUCTION  
1.1  SITE LOCATION AND PROJECTION DESCRIPTION  
The Show Low Mountain Ranch development is located on B ourdon Ranch about 4 
miles north U. S. Route 60 in Navajo County. The project site is located south and west 
of Cooley Knoll.  
The proposed development is approximately 301.3 acres, whi ch will consisting of 6.8 
acres of commercial, 178.2 acres of RV/PM Resort (appro x. 350 units) 29.5 acres of 
RV/PM Park and 86.8 acres of MH/RV community.  
To the south is the Bourbon Ranch Estates, a detached s ingle-family development 
consisting of large 2+ acre lots, to the east is Bourdo n Ranch Road with undeveloped 
State Land beyond. To the northeast is a cinder quarry a nd the Laguna Estates 
subdivision, consisting of 1/3 acre single-single fam ily lots. To the west and north is 
vacant state land. To the southwest is Rocky Arroyo, a  large wash that is situated at 
least 45-feet below the average elevation of the project sit e. With exception of the 
previously mentioned wash, no significant waterways ar e identifiable on the project 
site. A Vicinity Map is included in Appendix A. 
1.2  PURPOSE AND OBJECTIVES  
The purpose of this report is to provide preliminary drainage information to support the 
Show Low Mountain Ranch Master Plan Update and the fu ture development of the 
site. This report will discuss the development standards  and concepts that will be 
incorporated into the future design of the development and  provide a hydrologic 
analysis of the existing conditions found in and around the project site.  
1.3  FEMA FIRM INSURANCE RATE MAP  
The site is located on Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) National Flood 
Insurance Program (NFIP), Flood Insurance Rate Maps (FIRM) No. 04017C4504E, and 
FIRM No. 04017C4525E, both with effective dates of September 26, 2008 (see Exhibit 
2a & 2b). The majority of the project is located in Flo od Hazard Zone X with a portion 
in Zone A along Rocky Arroyo in the southwest corner of the site. A copy of the effective 
flood plains is included as Exhibit 2a & 2b in the Appendix A. These zones are defined 
as follows: 
Zone X, is defined as: “Areas determined to be outside of th e 0.2% 
annual chance floodplain.” 
Zone A is defined as “Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHAs) subject to 
inundation by the 1% annual chance flood. No Base Flo od Elevations 
determined.” 
It should be noted that this project will design around the SFHA’s and has no intent to 
re-delineate the effective floodplains. Areas of Flood Zone A  are located within the 
Rocky Arroyo and due to the significant topographic relief, will not be disturbed during 
the development of this site.

1.4  KNOWN DEVELOPMENT REQUIREMENTS  
The project lies within Navajo County and will be designed to conform with the Navajo 
County Drainage Policy. The Navajo County’s policy st ates that “All developments 
within Navajo County shall provide such storm draina ge facilities as are necessary to 
ensure that all improvements, structures and properties, b oth within the subject 
development and those located up and downstream of the devel opment, shall be 
protected from the adverse impact of storm water due to th e proposed development. 
The storm drainage facilities shall be designed and const ructed so as to ensure that 
the post-development flow from the development site is not g reater than the pre-
development flow for the 2-, 10-, 50- and 100-year flood events.” 
1.5  PREVIOUS STUDIES  
A previous drainage report has been prepared for the development of this site by Tetra-
tech, dated 6/17/2009. This report was prepared for the Bourdon Ranch 
Development, LLC. Some portions of constructed were started  and it appears that 
some rough grading was performed on site prior to the pr oject being halted. As 
Previously stated, this preliminary drainage report is t o support the Show Low 
Mountain Ranch Master Plan Update. While some of the in formation within the Tetra-
tech may still be valid, the proposed product and layou t are anticipated to be 
completely different. This preliminary report is anticip ated to replaced previously 
prepared reports for this site.  
1.6  HAZARD EROSION SETBACKS  
Erosion hazard setbacks are shown on Exhibit 3a – Ex isting Conditions HEC-HMS 
Schematic for Rocky Arroyo extending through Show Low Mountain Ranch. The erosion 
hazard setback distance was calculated from the Arizona State Standard 5-96, level 1 
analysis. The erosion setback distance is measured from the estimated floodplain limit 
as calculated per the Arizona Department of Transportation Highway Drainage Design 
Manual – Hydraulics, 2007. The lot layout in the develo pment will be designed such 
that a majority of lots are located at or beyond top of banks. Lot fill or grading which 
encroach the erosion hazard setbacks shall provide rein forcement of the banks with 
either rip rap and/or scour walls.  
2.0  OFFSITE DRAINAGE  
2.1  OFFSITE DRAINAGE   
The project site is impacted by offsite flows. The general slope of the land flows from 
Southeast to northwest. Northeast of the site is Cooley Knoll. Runoff from this feature 
will enter the project site via the northeast and north pr operty lines. Generally, runoff 
from Cooley Knoll will enter the site and flow to the no rthwest, exiting the site in one

<!-- page 952 -->
SHOW LOW MOUNTAIN RANCH 
PRELIMINARY DRAINAGE REPORT 
SHOW LOW, NAVAHO COUNTY, ARIZONA 
 
  Atwell |  2 
 
of three discharge locations. To the south is the Bourdon Ranch Estates Development. 
Runoff from this development will enter the project site vi a sheet flow. A low ridge, 
located approximately in the middle of the east portion o f the site will direct runoff to 
the northwest or northeast. In the northeast corner of t he eastern portion of the site, 
there exists a 3-barrel culvert that directs runoff under Bourdon Ranch Road from 
which the runoff continues east toward an un-named wash and eventually Silver Creek. 
Runoff from the western portion of the site will flow toward Rocky Arroyo.  
An Existing Conditions model was prepared using avail able soils data, land use data 
and rainfall data from the NOAA Atlas 14 data base. T hese values were processed for 
the drainage basins and the HEC-HMS V4.9 program was u sed to estimate the peak 
flows for the 2-, 10-, 50- and 100-year storm events.  
2.1.A  RAINFALL LOSSES  
Per the ADOT Drainage Design Manual – Hydrology, The Green-Ampt methodology was 
used to estimate rainfall losses. The Green-Ampt loss rate parameters include: 
1.  Surface Retention (IA) 
2.  Effective Porosity (DTHETA) 
3.  Wetting Front Soil Suction Head (PSIF) 
4.  Hydraulic Conductivity (XKSAT) 
5.  Percent Impervious Cover (RTIMP) 
The surface retention was estimate using Table 3-1 from the ADOT Hydrology Manual. 
Effective porosity was determined using Table 3-2 from t he ADOT Hydrology Manual, 
based on a log-weighted value of the hydraulic conducti vity and soil types located 
within the drainage basins. The soil types were determined using the ADOT SSURGO 
Soil data base, which is a simplified version of the USGS’s Web Soil Survey data base. 
There are two different soil types located within the study area. The soil around Cooley 
Knoll is loamy sand (AZ633-35), while the rest of the st ie has silty clay loam (AZ633-
65). The wetting front soil suction head is also prov ided in the ADOT soil data base. 
The hydraulic conductivity was adjusted to account fo r the land use for the existing 
conditions and also for the vegetative cover. The percent  impervious cover was 
estimated using Table 3-3 of the ADOT Hydrology Manual and was based on the land 
use in the current, existing conditions. Calculations t ables are provided in Appendix B 
of this report.  
2.1.B  UNIT  HYDROGRAPH  
In accordance with the ADOT Hydrology Manual, the Clark Unit Hydrograph method was 
used to estimate hydrograph parameters for each rainfall event. Clark Unit Hydrograph

<!-- page 953 -->
SHOW LOW MOUNTAIN RANCH 
PRELIMINARY DRAINAGE REPORT 
SHOW LOW, NAVAHO COUNTY, ARIZONA 
 
  Atwell |  3 
 
parameters include the time of concentration, a storage coefficient and a time-area 
relationship. The “Desert-Mountain” time of concentratio n equation (ADOT Eqn. 4.1) 
was used to determine the time of concentration for the existing drainage basins. The 
“Default” time-area relationship was also used. The storage coefficient was calculated 
using the ADOT Equation 4.4. See Appendix B for the Time  of Concentration 
calculations.  
For the Rocky Arroyo drainage area, soil data is not available for the majority of the 
drainage basin, therefore the USGS StreamStats program wa s used to estimate the 
peak flow in and contributing drainage areas of the w ash. The ADOT Regression 
equations (ADOT Table 11-4) was also used to estimate th e peak flows in the wash. 
The Regression equation was found to derive a peak flow higher than the StreamStats 
program and will be used in the future design. 
3.0  ONSITE DRAINAGE  
The drainage plan to manage the runoff generated onsite is that the residential lots 
will drain toward the streets. The streets will drain t oward detention basins located 
near the historical discharge points, as identified in t he existing conditions model. 
These detention basins will be sized to maintain developed discharge at or below the 
existing conditions peak flow for the 2-, 10-, 50- and  100-year storm events. 
Throughout the development process a proposed conditions model will be prepared 
using the HEC-HMS program to verify the performance of each detention basin.  
3.1  DRAINAGE CONVEYANCE  
The majority of the on-site runoff will be conveyed in the road and roadway ditches. On 
areas of the development that require a larger conveyance, d rainage channels will 
either convey runoff to a nearby road and ditch, detention basin or offsite. The majority 
of the lots that are located on the edges of the property boundary, may not require 
drainage improvements as the existing topography shows that the runoff will travel 
offsite. This is considered to be an acceptable approach as the adjacent roads will cut-
off any upstream portions of the existing drainage basi ns, effectively reducing the 
contributing runoff. The roads, roadway ditches and small drainage channels will be 
graded in such a manner to convey runoff towards the de tention basins, or drainage 
easements that will be located onsite.  
3.2  EROSION PROTECTION  
During subsequential studies, channel velocities will be evaluated. Some of the smaller 
drainage ditches may not require bank protection, given t he rocky terrain and 
anticipated lower velocities. Channel that are found to require erosion protection will

<!-- page 954 -->
SHOW LOW MOUNTAIN RANCH 
PRELIMINARY DRAINAGE REPORT 
SHOW LOW, NAVAHO COUNTY, ARIZONA 
 
  Atwell |  4 
 
be provided with loose riprap designed in accordance with  HEC-15 or similar analysis 
methodology.  
4.0  HYDR AULIC IMPROVEMENTS AND HYDRAULIC STRUCTURES  
4.1  ONSITE DRAINAGE CONCEPTS  
On-site rainfall runoff from the street will be routed v ia in-street flow to low points in 
the road where depressions or catch basins with storm drain systems will be installed 
to collect flows and discharge runoff into proposed de tention basins. Final design 
calculations will be included in the final design docum ents to support the proposed 
improvements.  
4.2  OFFSITE DRAINAGE CONVEY ANCE  
Improvements to Rocky Arroyo are not anticipated to be included with the development 
of Show Low Mountain Ranch. An existing conditions study was performed on the wash 
to evaluate the developable area adjacent to the wash. HEC-R AS V6.2 was used to 
estimate the water surface elevation within the wash and to delineate the anticipated 
100-year flood limits. Reports from the HEC-RAS progra m are included in Appendix B 
of this report.  
An erosion hazard area has been established to setback and protect any development 
from potential erosion within the Rocky Arroyo wash. T his set back distance was 
established using the Level 1 analysis according to the ADWR state standard 5-96. The 
peak flow within the wash was estimated to be 4,550 cfs , and the wash is relatively 
straight, therefore the setback distance is estimated to be 67 feet.  
5.0  STORM WATER  STORAGE FACILITIES  
Show Low Mountain Ranch will implement onsite storm water storage facilities as a means to 
maintain 100-year proposed condition peak flows at or below existing condition levels.  
The proposed land use condition hydrologic analysis (p resented in subsequent reports) will 
reflect a pre and post-development land use condition anal ysis incorporating a series of 
basins which attenuates peak flows exiting Show Low Mountain Ranch to at or below existing 
condition levels.  
The conceptual storm water storage facilities presented herein are discussed in further detail 
below.  
5.1  DETENTION BASIN DESIGN  
The proposed condition hydrologic analysis reflects con ceptual storm water storage 
basins distributed throughout Show Low Mountain Ranch as a means to treat the first 
flush runoff and to mitigate increases in peak flow.

5.2  DETENTION BASIN OUTLETS  
As the majority of the basins throughout Show Low Mou ntain Ranch will be detention 
basins, an engineered outlet structure will be provided i n each basin to convey up to 
the 100-year flows to the adjacent wash and or historic al discharge location. Final 
design of the outlet storm piping will be conducted with the final design documents for 
the subdivision. Maximum ponding was set so that the 100-year peak stage was no 
more than 1-foot above the grate inlet.  
5.3  BASIN OUTFALLS  
Each basin has been designed to have a controlled outfall  location. Generally, these 
are located such that in an extreme storm event (greater th an the 100-year storm) or 
in back-to-back event, excess stormwater will convey thro ugh and out of the site 
without negatively impacting the residential structures.  
5.4  FINISHED FLOORS  
The proposed residential lots will be designed to be plac ed at least 12-inches above 
the adjacent 100-year water surface, 12-inches above the b asin outfall elevation, or 
12-inches above the low top of curb.

6.0  SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS  
The following conclusions are based on Navajo County Drainage Policy requirements.  
1)  The hydrologic analysis used herein is based on the analy sis presented ADOT 
Hydrology Drainage Design Manual.  
2)  Proposed inlets and storm drains will be appropriately sized to accommodate the 100-
year event. 
3)  Storm water storage facilities for this project are sized to attenuate the developed peak 
flow to at or below existing conditions and convey the 100year peak flows. 
4)  Storm water storage facilities basin has a designated o utfall path to convey extreme 
storms or back-to-back events. 
5)  Finished floors will be vertically located at least 12-i nches above the adjacent 100-
year water surface, 12-inches above the basin outfall eleva tion, or 12-inches above 
the low top of curb.

Preface
Soil surveys contain information that affects land use planning in survey areas. 
They highlight soil limitations that affect various land uses and provide information 
about the properties of the soils in the survey areas. Soil surveys are designed for 
many different users, including farmers, ranchers, foresters, agronomists, urban 
planners, community officials, engineers, developers, builders, and home buyers. 
Also, conservationists, teachers, students, and specialists in recreation, waste 
disposal, and pollution control can use the surveys to help them understand, 
protect, or enhance the environment.
Various land use regulations of Federal, State, and local governments may impose 
special restrictions on land use or land treatment. Soil surveys identify soil 
properties that are used in making various land use or land treatment decisions. 
The information is intended to help the land users identify and reduce the effects of 
soil limitations on various land uses. The landowner or user is responsible for 
identifying and complying with existing laws and regulations.
Although soil survey information can be used for general farm, local, and wider area 
planning, onsite investigation is needed to supplement this information in some 
cases. Examples include soil quality assessments (http://www.nrcs.usda.gov/wps/
portal/nrcs/main/soils/health/) and certain conservation and engineering 
applications. For more detailed information, contact your local USDA Service Center 
(https://offices.sc.egov.usda.gov/locator/app?agency=nrcs) or your NRCS State Soil 
Scientist (http://www.nrcs.usda.gov/wps/portal/nrcs/detail/soils/contactus/?
cid=nrcs142p2_053951).
Great differences in soil properties can occur within short distances. Some soils are 
seasonally wet or subject to flooding. Some are too unstable to be used as a 
foundation for buildings or roads. Clayey or wet soils are poorly suited to use as 
septic tank absorption fields. A high water table makes a soil poorly suited to 
basements or underground installations.
The National Cooperative Soil Survey is a joint effort of the United States 
Department of Agriculture and other Federal agencies, State agencies including the 
Agricultural Experiment Stations, and local agencies. The Natural Resources 
Conservation Service (NRCS) has leadership for the Federal part of the National 
Cooperative Soil Survey.
Information about soils is updated periodically. Updated information is available 
through the NRCS Web Soil Survey, the site for official soil survey information.

and where applicable, sex, marital status, familial status, parental status, religion, 
sexual orientation, genetic information, political beliefs, reprisal, or because all or a 
part of an individual's income is derived from any public assistance program. (Not 
all prohibited bases apply to all programs.) Persons with disabilities who require

How Soil Surveys Are Made
Soil surveys are made to provide information about the soils and miscellaneous 
areas in a specific area. They include a description of the soils and miscellaneous 
areas and their location on the landscape and tables that show soil properties and 
limitations affecting various uses. Soil scientists observed the steepness, length, 
and shape of the slopes; the general pattern of drainage; the kinds of crops and 
native plants; and the kinds of bedrock. They observed and described many soil 
profiles. A soil profile is the sequence of natural layers, or horizons, in a soil. The 
profile extends from the surface down into the unconsolidated material in which the 
soil formed or from the surface down to bedrock. The unconsolidated material is 
devoid of roots and other living organisms and has not been changed by other 
biological activity.
Currently, soils are mapped according to the boundaries of major land resource 
areas (MLRAs). MLRAs are geographically associated land resource units that 
share common characteristics related to physiography, geology, climate, water 
resources, soils, biological resources, and land uses (USDA, 2006). Soil survey 
areas typically consist of parts of one or more MLRA.
The soils and miscellaneous areas in a survey area occur in an orderly pattern that 
is related to the geology, landforms, relief, climate, and natural vegetation of the 
area. Each kind of soil and miscellaneous area is associated with a particular kind 
of landform or with a segment of the landform. By observing the soils and 
miscellaneous areas in the survey area and relating their position to specific 
segments of the landform, a soil scientist develops a concept, or model, of how they 
were formed. Thus, during mapping, this model enables the soil scientist to predict 
with a considerable degree of accuracy the kind of soil or miscellaneous area at a 
specific location on the landscape.
Commonly, individual soils on the landscape merge into one another as their 
characteristics gradually change. To construct an accurate soil map, however, soil 
scientists must determine the boundaries between the soils. They can observe only 
a limited number of soil profiles. Nevertheless, these observations, supplemented 
by an understanding of the soil-vegetation-landscape relationship, are sufficient to 
verify predictions of the kinds of soil in an area and to determine the boundaries.
Soil scientists recorded the characteristics of the soil profiles that they studied. They 
noted soil color, texture, size and shape of soil aggregates, kind and amount of rock 
fragments, distribution of plant roots, reaction, and other features that enable them 
to identify soils. After describing the soils in the survey area and determining their 
properties, the soil scientists assigned the soils to taxonomic classes (units). 
Taxonomic classes are concepts. Each taxonomic class has a set of soil 
characteristics with precisely defined limits. The classes are used as a basis for 
comparison to classify soils systematically. Soil taxonomy, the system of taxonomic 
classification used in the United States, is based mainly on the kind and character 
of soil properties and the arrangement of horizons within the profile. After the soil 
5

<!-- page 1036 -->
scientists classified and named the soils in the survey area, they compared the 
individual soils with similar soils in the same taxonomic class in other areas so that 
they could confirm data and assemble additional data based on experience and 
research.
The objective of soil mapping is not to delineate pure map unit components; the 
objective is to separate the landscape into landforms or landform segments that 
have similar use and management requirements. Each map unit is defined by a 
unique combination of soil components and/or miscellaneous areas in predictable 
proportions. Some components may be highly contrasting to the other components 
of the map unit. The presence of minor components in a map unit in no way 
diminishes the usefulness or accuracy of the data. The delineation of such 
landforms and landform segments on the map provides sufficient information for the 
development of resource plans. If intensive use of small areas is planned, onsite 
investigation is needed to define and locate the soils and miscellaneous areas.
Soil scientists make many field observations in the process of producing a soil map. 
The frequency of observation is dependent upon several factors, including scale of 
mapping, intensity of mapping, design of map units, complexity of the landscape, 
and experience of the soil scientist. Observations are made to test and refine the 
soil-landscape model and predictions and to verify the classification of the soils at 
specific locations. Once the soil-landscape model is refined, a significantly smaller 
number of measurements of individual soil properties are made and recorded. 
These measurements may include field measurements, such as those for color, 
depth to bedrock, and texture, and laboratory measurements, such as those for 
content of sand, silt, clay, salt, and other components. Properties of each soil 
typically vary from one point to another across the landscape.
Observations for map unit components are aggregated to develop ranges of 
characteristics for the components. The aggregated values are presented. Direct 
measurements do not exist for every property presented for every map unit 
component. Values for some properties are estimated from combinations of other 
properties.
While a soil survey is in progress, samples of some of the soils in the area generally 
are collected for laboratory analyses and for engineering tests. Soil scientists 
interpret the data from these analyses and tests as well as the field-observed 
characteristics and the soil properties to determine the expected behavior of the 
soils under different uses. Interpretations for all of the soils are field tested through 
observation of the soils in different uses and under different levels of management. 
Some interpretations are modified to fit local conditions, and some new 
interpretations are developed to meet local needs. Data are assembled from other 
sources, such as research information, production records, and field experience of 
specialists. For example, data on crop yields under defined levels of management 
are assembled from farm records and from field or plot experiments on the same 
kinds of soil.
Predictions about soil behavior are based not only on soil properties but also on 
such variables as climate and biological activity. Soil conditions are predictable over 
long periods of time, but they are not predictable from year to year. For example, 
soil scientists can predict with a fairly high degree of accuracy that a given soil will 
have a high water table within certain depths in most years, but they cannot predict 
that a high water table will always be at a specific level in the soil on a specific date.
After soil scientists located and identified the significant natural bodies of soil in the 
survey area, they drew the boundaries of these bodies on aerial photographs and 
Custom Soil Resource Report
6

<!-- page 1037 -->
identified each as a specific map unit. Aerial photographs show trees, buildings, 
fields, roads, and rivers, all of which help in locating boundaries accurately.
Custom Soil Resource Report
7

<!-- page 1038 -->
Soil Map
The soil map section includes the soil map for the defined area of interest, a list of 
soil map units on the map and extent of each map unit, and cartographic symbols 
displayed on the map. Also presented are various metadata about data used to 
produce the map, and a description of each soil map unit.

Map Unit Descriptions
The map units delineated on the detailed soil maps in a soil survey represent the 
soils or miscellaneous areas in the survey area. The map unit descriptions, along 
with the maps, can be used to determine the composition and properties of a unit.
A map unit delineation on a soil map represents an area dominated by one or more 
major kinds of soil or miscellaneous areas. A map unit is identified and named 
according to the taxonomic classification of the dominant soils. Within a taxonomic 
class there are precisely defined limits for the properties of the soils. On the 
landscape, however, the soils are natural phenomena, and they have the 
characteristic variability of all natural phenomena. Thus, the range of some 
observed properties may extend beyond the limits defined for a taxonomic class. 
Areas of soils of a single taxonomic class rarely, if ever, can be mapped without 
including areas of other taxonomic classes. Consequently, every map unit is made 
up of the soils or miscellaneous areas for which it is named and some minor 
components that belong to taxonomic classes other than those of the major soils.
Most minor soils have properties similar to those of the dominant soil or soils in the 
map unit, and thus they do not affect use and management. These are called 
noncontrasting, or similar, components. They may or may not be mentioned in a 
particular map unit description. Other minor components, however, have properties 
and behavioral characteristics divergent enough to affect use or to require different 
management. These are called contrasting, or dissimilar, components. They 
generally are in small areas and could not be mapped separately because of the 
scale used. Some small areas of strongly contrasting soils or miscellaneous areas 
are identified by a special symbol on the maps. If included in the database for a 
given area, the contrasting minor components are identified in the map unit 
descriptions along with some characteristics of each. A few areas of minor 
components may not have been observed, and consequently they are not 
mentioned in the descriptions, especially where the pattern was so complex that it 
was impractical to make enough observations to identify all the soils and 
miscellaneous areas on the landscape.
The presence of minor components in a map unit in no way diminishes the 
usefulness or accuracy of the data. The objective of mapping is not to delineate 
pure taxonomic classes but rather to separate the landscape into landforms or 
landform segments that have similar use and management requirements. The 
delineation of such segments on the map provides sufficient information for the 
development of resource plans. If intensive use of small areas is planned, however, 
Custom Soil Resource Report
11

<!-- page 1042 -->
onsite investigation is needed to define and locate the soils and miscellaneous 
areas.
An identifying symbol precedes the map unit name in the map unit descriptions. 
Each description includes general facts about the unit and gives important soil 
properties and qualities.
Soils that have profiles that are almost alike make up a soil series. Except for 
differences in texture of the surface layer, all the soils of a series have major 
horizons that are similar in composition, thickness, and arrangement.
Soils of one series can differ in texture of the surface layer, slope, stoniness, 
salinity, degree of erosion, and other characteristics that affect their use. On the 
basis of such differences, a soil series is divided into soil phases. Most of the areas 
shown on the detailed soil maps are phases of soil series. The name of a soil phase 
commonly indicates a feature that affects use or management. For example, Alpha 
silt loam, 0 to 2 percent slopes, is a phase of the Alpha series.
Some map units are made up of two or more major soils or miscellaneous areas. 
These map units are complexes, associations, or undifferentiated groups.
A complex consists of two or more soils or miscellaneous areas in such an intricate 
pattern or in such small areas that they cannot be shown separately on the maps. 
The pattern and proportion of the soils or miscellaneous areas are somewhat similar 
in all areas. Alpha-Beta complex, 0 to 6 percent slopes, is an example.
An association is made up of two or more geographically associated soils or 
miscellaneous areas that are shown as one unit on the maps. Because of present 
or anticipated uses of the map units in the survey area, it was not considered 
practical or necessary to map the soils or miscellaneous areas separately. The 
pattern and relative proportion of the soils or miscellaneous areas are somewhat 
similar. Alpha-Beta association, 0 to 2 percent slopes, is an example.
An undifferentiated group is made up of two or more soils or miscellaneous areas 
that could be mapped individually but are mapped as one unit because similar 
interpretations can be made for use and management. The pattern and proportion 
of the soils or miscellaneous areas in a mapped area are not uniform. An area can 
be made up of only one of the major soils or miscellaneous areas, or it can be made 
up of all of them. Alpha and Beta soils, 0 to 2 percent slopes, is an example.
Some surveys include miscellaneous areas. Such areas have little or no soil 
material and support little or no vegetation. Rock outcrop is an example.

Lōkahi, LLC (Lōkahi) has 
prepared a Traffic Statement 
for the proposed Show Low

for submittal to Navajo 
County. The proposed 
development is located near 
the northwest corner of 
Bourdon Ranch Road and 
Roundup Drive in Show Low, 
Arizona and will consist of an 
RV resort with 350 spaces, 96 
cottage units, and a 
manufactured home 
community with 312 lots. See 
Figure 1  for the vicinity map. 
See Figure 2 for the site plan. 
 
Per ADOT TGP 240, a Category 
I analysis would typically be 
required based on the

and unsignalized intersections within a 0.5 mile, of which none exist. Therefore, it is

recommended that a Traffic Statement be accepted in lieu of a Category I Analysis, due to the 
remote location of the proposed development. The objective of this Traffic Impact Statement 
is to evaluate the proposed development’s traffic related impacts to the site access driveways 
in the opening year. 
 
EXISTING CONDITIONS 
The project area consists of 297.7 acres, located approximately 4 miles north of US 60 and 5 
miles east of SR 77. The existing site is currently vacant land with Special Development (SD) 
zoning. The site is generally surrounded by vacant land and rural residential lots.  
 
Bourdon Ranch Road is a north-south roadway that provides one (1) through lane in each 
direction of travel and offers an alternate route to SR 77 between Show Low and Taylor. 
According to the Southern Navajo/Apache County Sub-Regional Transportation Plan , dated 
September 2007, Bourdon Ranch Road is classified as a County Minor Arterial. According to the 
Northern Arizona Council of Governments (NACOG) Transportation Data Management System, 
the daily traffic reported along Bourdon Ranch Road, north of US 60 (Location ID NNA-054), in 
2022 was a total of 1,969 vehicles-per-day (vpd). There is a posted speed limit of 50 miles per 
hour (mph). 
 
Roundup Drive  is an unpaved local roadway that provides one (1) lane in each direction of 
travel. Roundup Drive terminates approximately 1 mile west of Bourdon Ranch Road. 
 
PR OPOSED DEVELOPMENT 
The proposed Show Low Mountain 
Ranch development will consist of an 
RV resort with 350 spaces, 96 
cottage units, and a manufactured 
home community with 312 lots. The 
opening year is anticipated to occur 
in the year 2026. See 
Attachment A 
and Figure 2 for the site plan.  
 
Access to the Show Low Mountain 
Ranch development will primarily be 
from two (2) full access driveways 
along Bourdon Ranch Road. A 
secondary full access is proposed on 
the southern border of the site via 
Roundup Drive. The first driveway 
proposed along Bourdon Ranch

<!-- page 1056 -->

Coast2Coast Equities, Inc.  
Show Low Mountain Ranch  
Road is located approximately 640 feet north of Roundup Drive and will serve as a full access 
major entry for the entire Show Low Mountain Ranch development. The second driveway is 
located approximately 1,500 feet north of Roundup Drive and will serve as a full access gated 
entry to the RV resort.  
 
TRIP GENER ATION 
The trip generation for the proposed development was calculated utilizing the Institute of 
Transportation Engineers (ITE) publication entitled Trip Generation, 11 th  Edition . The ITE rates are 
based on studies that measured the trip generation characteristics for various types of land 
uses. The rates are expressed in terms of trips per unit of land use type. This publication is 
considered to be the standard for the transportation engineering profession.

Mountain Lake Area, dated April 2, 2008. The proposed site was previously approved as a 
single-family housing development. The trip generation for the previously approved 
development is shown in Table 1. See Attachment B for traffic impact analysis.

TUR N LANE WARR ANT 
Turn lanes or auxiliary lanes, allow vehicles exiting a roadway to slow to a reduced speed to 
execute a turn without impeding the main flow of traffic. The  ADOT Traffic Guidelines and 
Processes (TGP 245) , dated January 2019, was used to determine the need for turn lanes along 
Bourdon Ranch Road.  
 
RIGHT TURN LANE WARRANTS 
According to TGP 245 a right turn lane is required when the following criteria shown in the table 
are met. 
 
Table 4 – Right Turn Lane Warrant 
 
 
 
Bourdon Ranch Road currently has 
one (1) through lane  in each direction and a posted speed of 
50 mph . According to the NACOG Transportation Data Management System, the peak hour 
traffic volume along Bourdon Ranch Road (Location ID NNA-054) in the southbound direction 
was a total of 115 vehicles-per-hour (vph). Using a 2.0% annual growth rate, the southbound 
traffic volumes are anticipated to be 125 vph in the opening year of the proposed development. 
 
The growth rate was derived from the United States Census Bureau population estimations for 
Navajo County; the population percent change from April 1, 2020, to July 1, 2022, was reported 
as 1.8%. As a conservative approach, a 2.0% annual growth rate was applied to the existing 
traffic volumes through the opening year, projected in 2026, to estimate the traffic growth on 
Bourdon Ranch Road.

Based on the table, right turn lanes are not warranted at the site driveways. Additionally, it is 
assumed that US 60 will be the primary route to Bourdon Ranch Road to ultimately access the 
site. Southbound entering trips are not expected to be likely and therefore vehicles executing 
southbound right turns to enter the site are anticipated to be minimal. 
 
LEFT TURN LANE WARRANTS 
According to TGP 245 a left turn lane is required when the following criteria shown in the table 
are met. 
 
Table 5 – Left Turn Lane Warrant 
 
 
 
Bourdon Ranch Road currently has 
one (1) through lane  in each direction and a posted speed of 
50 mph . According to the NACOG Transportation Data Management System, the peak hour 
traffic volume along Bourdon Ranch Road (Location ID NNA-054) in the northbound direction 
was a total of 110 vehicles-per-hour (vph). Using a 2.0% annual growth rate, the southbound 
traffic volumes are anticipated to be 119 vph in the opening year of the proposed development. 
 
Based on the table, a minimum of 15 peak hour left turns will warrant a left turn lane. It is 
anticipated that both site driveways along Bourdon Ranch Road will meet these minimum 
criteria, therefore left turn lanes are warranted and recommended at the two (2) site driveways 
proposed along Bourdon Ranch Road.

TUR N LANE DESIGN 
ADOT TGP 430 provides guidance for designing left turn lanes.  
 
LEFT TURN LANES 
According to Section 430.1, a left turn lane consists of a taper, gap, and storage. The following 
calculations are based on Figure 430-C. 
 
• 300-foot taper  (50 mph x 12 ft lane/2) 
o It is assumed the left turn lanes will be constructed with symmetrical widening.  
• 60-foot gap  (Table 430-1 x 2/3) 
• 145-foot storage  (minimum braking distance + queue – gap difference) 
o 120-foot minimum braking distance (Table 430-2) 
o 85-foot queue ((72 vph + 120 vph)/2) / 30 periods/hr x 25 feet)  
The average AM and PM peak hour entering turning volumes for the entire site were 
conservatively used to calculate a maximum queue length of 80 feet. Per TGP 430, 
the minimum queue length for all traffic control situations should accommodate 
two passenger vehicles or one passenger vehicle and one truck. Due to the need for 
recreational vehicles to access the site, an 85-foot minimum queue length is 
recommended, which accommodates one passenger vehicle and one truck. 
o 30-foot gap difference (Figure 430-C.) 
 
SUMMAR Y 
The proposed Show Low Mountain Ranch is located near the northwest corner of Bourdon 
Ranch Road and Roundup Drive in Show Low, Arizona. The proposed development consists of 
an RV resort with 350 spaces, 96 cottage units, and a manufactured home community with 312 
lots and is anticipated to generate 2,608 weekday trips, with 163 trips occurring during the AM 
peak hour and 211 trips during the PM peak hour. Per ADOT TGP 240, a Category I analysis would 
typically be required based on the anticipated peak hour trips. A Category I analysis includes 
two (2) study horizon years with an analysis of major signalized and unsignalized intersections 
within a 0.5 mile, of which none exist. The nearest major unsignalized intersection is located 
over 3.5 miles south at the intersection of US 60 and Bourdon Ranch Road. Therefore, it is 
recommended that a Traffic Statement be accepted in lieu of a Category I Analysis, due to the 
remote location of the proposed development. 
 
Access to the proposed development will primarily be from two (2) full access driveways along 
Bourdon Ranch Road. A secondary full access is proposed on the southern border of the site via 
Roundup Drive. It is assumed that the majority of trips accessing the site will enter and exit 
from US 60. Therefore, based on the projected traffic volumes on Bourdon Ranch Road and 
unlikely southbound right turning traffic, right turn lanes are not warranted or recommended. 
Left turn lanes are warranted and recommended at both site driveways located along Bourdon

Ranch Road. Per Figure 430-C within ADOT TGP 430, it is recommended that the left turn lanes 
are constructed with 300-foot tapers, 60-foot gaps, and 145-foot storage. It is assumed the left 
turn lanes will be constructed with symmetrical widening. 
 
According to Table 2.1: Roadway Planning Level Traffic Volumes  within the MCDOT Roadway 
Design Manual , dated March 2023, an undivided urban and rural minor arterial with two (2) 
lanes is expected to achieve desired LOS with 13,500 vpd and 10,400 vpd, respectively. With a 
2.0% annual growth rate and the build-out of the proposed development, Bourdon Ranch Road 
is anticipated to carry approximately 4,700 vpd. This results in an available capacity of 
approximately 65% for if Bourdon Ranch Road is considered as an undivided urban minor 
arterial and an available capacity of approximately 55% if considered as an undivided rural 
minor arterial.  
 
In conclusion, the traffic generated by the proposed Show Low Mountain Ranch development 
is anticipated to result in minimal traffic related impacts to the existing roadway network and 
the surrounding area. Therefore, it is not expected that additional analysis would result in 
further recommendations.
